abajo.note: In an address, abajo means west - where the sun goes down

acuerdo.note: Agree the fare before you get in. Always

ahorita.note: Not a length of time. It states an intention, and the tone tells you which

albergar.note: 'Albergar una esperanza' = to harbor a hope

albur.note: A pun with a hidden, often cheeky, second meaning

almuerzo.note: At twelve, and the big meal of the day

amanecer.en: to stay up till dawn / dawn

amar.note: Bigger than querer, and used far less. Many never say it

amañarse.note: To grow attached to a place

amor.note: 'Mi amor' is said to almost anybody, warmly

apoyar.note: Emotional support; 'te apoyo' = I support you

argumento.note: A point you make, not a fight

arriba.note: In an address, arriba means east - where the sun comes up

asimismo.note: Elegant way to add a point

aspirar.note: In Nica speech, the 's' is aspirated or dropped

bicho.note: Informal — a bug, or affectionately a kid

bolsa.note: Water and juice are sold in bags here, not bottles

buena onda.note: 'Es buena onda' = he's a cool/kind person

buenas.note: Short for buenos días/buenas tardes. The everyday Nica greeting

cae bien.note: 'Me cae bien' = I like him/her (as a person)

cafecito.note: Diminutive of café — warmth, not size

calmarse.note: Telling somebody to is pouring petrol on it

calor.note: 'Hace calor' = it's hot. 'Tengo calor' = I'm hot

camión.note: In Mexico = bus; in Nicaragua a bus is 'bus'

captar.note: To catch a meaning or hint

carcajada.note: 'Soltar la carcajada' = to burst out laughing

chele.note: Nica slang. Not offensive. Fem: chela

chinear.en: to carry and fuss over a child
chinear.note: More than carrying. Carrying with affection

chunche.note: Any object whose name you do not know. Gets you out of anything

ciento.note: Used in compound numbers: ciento treinta = 130

comedor.note: A house with tables. You point at the pots

comprender.note: A touch more formal than entender

conceder.note: In debate, to grant a point

cuadra.note: Distances here are counted in cuadras, corner to corner

córdoba.note: The currency. Written córdoba, said peso

delicado.note: Nobody says grave out loud. Saying it seems like calling it

disculpa.note: Three parts: what you did, that it was your fault, what you will do

doble sentido.note: A phrase with a hidden, often cheeky, second meaning

dominar.note: 'Dominar un idioma' = to master a language

encantar.note: Stronger than gustar. 'Me encanta' = I love it

fiado.note: Buying now, paying later — common at pulperías

formulario.note: A paper form to fill out

fritanga.note: Sets up at dusk. You eat standing in the street

fíjate.note: 'Fíjate que...' = a classic way to start telling news

gallopinto.note: Nica national dish: rice and beans fried together

gordo.note: Not an insult here. Also used as an endearment

gustar.note: Me gusta = I like (it pleases me)

habría.note: Conditional perfect: 'habría hecho' = I would have done

hogar.note: Home as a feeling, warmer than 'casa'

hubiera.note: Past subjunctive: 'si hubiera sabido' = if I had known

huele.note: From oler, to smell. 'Huele a' = it smells like

ideay.note: Uniquely Nicaraguan. Means whatever the tone means

invierno.note: Means the rains, not cold. It is hot all year

jaña.note: Casual Nica slang for a girl or girlfriend

jodido.note: 'Qué jodido' - what a pain. Very common, mildly coarse

lago.note: 'Al lago' means north - the lake is north of Managua

maje.note: Like 'dude' — affectionate among friends, rude with strangers

mandado.note: Being sent on one means you belong to the house

mantener.note: 'Mantener mi punto' = to hold my point

moraleja.note: The lesson of a story or fable

mujer.note: 'Mi mujer' is the ordinary word here and carries none of the English weight

nacatamal.note: Sunday food. Bought early or it is gone

ojalá.note: Heard constantly. Everything you want and do not control

oído.note: The trained ear for understanding speech

parada.note: Often just a corner with people waiting

parece.note: ¿Qué te parece? = What do you think?

pega.note: 'Echarse un pega' = take a short nap

perdonar.note: Apologise once. Repeating it loads it back on them

pillar.note: To catch on to a joke or meaning

pinche.note: In Nica: stingy or low-quality (milder than Mexican usage)

pinolero.note: From pinol, from maize. What Nicaraguans call themselves

platica.note: 'Platicar' = to chat. Common in Central America

platicar.note: Common in Central America for casual talk

por ende.note: Formal connector, more refined than 'por eso'

puente.note: Often figurative: a bridge between worlds

pulpería.note: Somebody's front room with a grille. Sells anything, in any quantity

quizás.note: Often a soft 'no' in social contexts

reclamo.note: 'Hacer un reclamo' = to make a complaint

refresco.note: Water with fruit, not a fizzy drink. Always sweet

refrán.note: A traditional fixed saying — beloved in daily speech

regatear.note: Clothes and taxis yes. Food, buses and the pulpería never

registro.note: Formal vs informal level of language

relajo.note: 'Echar relajo' = to goof around, have fun

retruécano.note: A clever reversal of words for effect

saludar.note: Not greeting somebody you pass is the rudest thing you can do

sano.note: Humor that's 'sano' is good-natured, not crude

saudade.note: A bittersweet longing — borrowed feeling, deeply felt

suegra.note: Usted forever, even after she calls you mijo

tuviera.note: Past subjunctive of tener: 'si tuviera' = if I had

vacilar.note: Done to the people you like. Being spared it means you are still a guest

vigorón.en: yuca, chicharrón and curtido on a leaf

vos.note: Nica uses vos not tú. Changes conjugations

voseo.note: The vos pronoun system, universal in Nicaragua

árbol.note: Trees that were cut down decades ago are still used as addresses

abril.note: The hottest month in Nicaragua, at the end of the dry season

acertar.en: to get it right, to land it

achiote.note: The red seed paste that colours Nicaraguan meat

acostarse.en: to lie down/to go to bed

adoptivo.note: Nica adoptivo - said about you, never to you

agrio.note: Naranja agria - sour orange, used the way lemon is elsewhere

aguante.note: What the priest talks about at a wedding, more than love

ah.note: Recognition, not surprise. 'Áh, sí' = oh, right

aire.note: 'No tiene aire' about a car means no air conditioning

ajeno.note: Sentirse ajeno - to feel you are from elsewhere

alegría.note: '¿Quién causa tanta alegría?' - the Gritería call

alfombra.note: In Semana Santa, a carpet of dyed sawdust laid in the street for the procession to walk over

altar.note: Built in the front room for La Purísima

antorcha.note: Run from Guatemala hand to hand, arriving for the fifteenth

apellido.note: You have two: father's first, mother's second

apodo.note: Everybody has one. You do not choose it

arrecho.note: Both, and the tone decides. Never with elders, never in front of a lady

ayudante.note: Shouts the route, takes the fare, never sits down

baho.note: Meat, plantain and yuca steamed in layers under plantain leaves. A house dish, never a restaurant one

bendición.note: Children ask elders for it as a greeting. 'Bendición' - 'Dios te bendiga'

borracho.note: A sad drunk is pitied, a fighting drunk loses his friends

brindar.note: Touch every bottle, and look them in the face

brindis.en: the little gift handed out at a Purisima door
brindis.note: Caps, limes, cajeta, sweets - a household saves for it all year

cachimbo.note: Stronger than monton. Among friends, not with the suegra

caponera.note: What people actually call it. Mototaxi is the paperwork word

caso.note: 'Hacer caso' - to do as you are told

celos.note: Not strange here. Denying them is what is strange

chancho.note: Nicaragua says chancho, not cerdo, for the live animal

chischil.note: The Purisima gift children fight over and mothers hate

chisme.note: The newspaper of the barrio, and it changes at every mouth

chismosa.note: Not a serious insult - a good one is useful

coco.note: Cooking with coco is Caribbean-coast, not Managua

compadre.note: A family you choose. More than a friend, and it does not end

componer.note: Nicaragua mends things. Buying a new one is odd

copia.note: Bring two of everything. Nobody will tell you which

copla.note: What the Enano Cabezon shouts at your door in December

costeño.note: Half the country, and a different set of languages

criollo.note: The English-based language of Bluefields - not Spanish

cuarentena.en: the forty days after a birth
cuarentena.note: She does nothing. Her mother moves in

cumbia.note: The first thing they put on. The step is in the hips

defenderse.en: to get by/to hold your own
defenderse.note: The verb used for coping here, as if living were something you stand up to

devoto.note: Somebody paying a promise to a saint with their body

diminutivo.note: Does not shrink the thing. It brings it closer

dirección.note: An address here is landmarks, not a street and number

doler.note: The pain happens to you: 'me duele la cabeza', not 'I have a headache'

educación.note: 'Mala educación' means bad manners, not bad schooling

enano.note: El Enano Cabezon - the big-headed boy who recites beside the Gigantona

encargar.en: to order, to ask somebody to bring
encargar.note: You encargar from a neighbour, not from a business

exagerar.note: Not lying - a story is expected to grow in the telling

fama.note: Every barrio has one, and it is put there by people who never went in

fiar.note: Doña Chepa's notebook holds half the street

fijarse.note: 'Fíjese que' warns you a no is coming

gallo pinto.note: The national breakfast. Eaten most mornings of most lives

gigantona.note: The three-metre dancing doll of the December streets, strongest in Leon

gracia.note: Tener gracia is to be funny, not to be graceful

gritería.note: December 7. The whole country goes door to door shouting the answer

hallarse.en: to feel at home in a place
hallarse.note: No me hallo - you do not fit here, and nobody asks you to explain why

hoja.note: A plantain leaf is the plate at a fritanga

imagen.note: Not a photograph - the wooden figure of a saint carried in a procession

interlocal.note: Leaves when it is full, not at a time

letanía.note: The sung part of the Purisima, after the shouted question

luz.note: 'Se fue la luz' - the power went. Said with no drama at all

mapa.note: Of limited use in a city with no street names

medir.note: Medir es de gente que no sabe - a cook with sazon measures nothing

mijo.note: From 'mi hijo'. Warmth, not literal. Being called it means something

muletilla.note: pues, va, fijate, ideay - what holds a conversation up

muñeco.note: The ano viejo muneco sits on the pavement and burns at midnight

ofensa.note: Not the same as a hurt - an ofensa is public and it keeps

padrino.note: Each pays for one thing. That is how a wedding happens without money

panga.note: How you finish the journey to Bluefields

patio.note: Often has no wall. The neighbours' patio is the same patio

patria.note: September is 'el mes de la patria'

peso.note: What everyone actually calls a córdoba out loud

pila.note: Cement tank kept full. You never get in it - you scoop from it

pinolillo.note: The national drink. Stir it or you drink sweet water

pista.note: Two chairs moved aside is already a pista

portón.note: Where the real goodbye happens - the only place with no witnesses

prisa.note: 'Tengo prisa' - I am in a hurry. Rarely useful here

pésame.note: 'Mi pésame' and a handshake. Not that she is in a better place

pólvora.note: Nicaraguan polvora is about noise, not light

quesillo.en: cheese in a tortilla with cream and onion

quinceañera.en: a girl turning fifteen, and her party

quincena.note: The 15th and the 30th. The whole city changes on those days

recarga.note: Bought at any pulpería, by phone number

recomendar.note: Worth more than a CV. Whoever recommends you answers for you

remesa.note: Money from a relative abroad. Half the street lives on it

rincón.note: Esquina is a street corner, rincon is an indoor one

robar.note: 'Me robaron' - it was stolen from me, never 'I lost it'

rondón.note: Caribbean coast stew: fish, yuca, plantain and coconut milk

ruta.note: Managua buses are rutas, by number. Never 'camión'

sazón.en: the hand of the person cooking
sazón.note: Not the recipe and not the ingredients. Two women with the same pot do not get the same thing

serenata.note: Sung to mothers at midnight on the twenty-ninth of May

seño.note: How you address a woman behind a counter

sonar.note: Stem-changing: suena. Used constantly about how a word lands

tanda.note: Ordered for the whole table, never for yourself

tercero.note: Shortens to 'tercer' before a masculine noun

terremoto.note: The 1972 earthquake flattened central Managua. The addresses outlived the buildings

tiburón.note: Lake Cocibolca had freshwater sharks. The old people still talk about them

tocar.note: 'Me toca' - it is my turn. Being whose turn it is means you are inside

tope.note: Managua, August 1: Santo Domingo comes down from Las Sierritas into the city

tortilla.note: Thick maize tortilla, not the thin Mexican kind

uva.note: Twelve at midnight, one wish with each

vacilón.note: From vacilar. Teasing done as affection - the one nobody vacila is the one nobody knows

vals.note: Danced with the father first, at the quince

vara.note: Ni de vara - not a chance, and not up for discussion

varilla.note: Left standing out of the roof on purpose. It means there will be a second floor one day

velorio.note: You go, even if you did not know them

volumen.note: Shouting means it still matters. Cold politeness is what is serious

voz.note: 'Nota de voz' - a voice note, how people actually talk

patterns.title: Voseo — The Nica 'You'
patterns.text:
Nicaragua uses 'vos' instead of 'tú'. This changes conjugations:

• Tú tienes → Vos tenés
• Tú quieres → Vos querés
• Tú sabes → Vos sabés

Pattern: stress the last syllable, drop -ie- stems.

Commands: stress final syllable:
• Mira → Mirá • Anda → Andá • Toma → Tomá

You'll never hear 'tú' in Nicaragua.

patterns.title: Ser vs Estar — Two 'Be' Verbs
patterns.text:
SER — permanent things:
• Soy de EEUU (origin)
• Es doctora (profession)
• Es grande (inherent quality)

ESTAR — temporary/location:
• Estoy en Managua (location)
• Estoy enfermo (temp state)
• Está bueno (right now)

If it can change → estar.
If it defines what something IS → ser.

patterns.title: Me gusta — Backwards 'Liking'
patterns.text:
English: 'I like the food'
Spanish: 'Me gusta la comida' (food pleases me)

Subject is FLIPPED:
• Me gusta el arroz (I like rice)
• Me gustan los mangos (I like mangos)
• ¿Te gusta Nicaragua?

Gusta = one thing. Gustan = multiple things.

patterns.title: Nica Directions — No Street Names
patterns.text:
Managua has no street names. Everything is landmarks + compass:

• '2 cuadras al norte del parque'
• Arriba = east (sun comes up)
• Abajo = west (sun goes down)
• Al lago = toward Lake Managua

'De la Rotonda, 3 arriba, 1 al sur, casa esquinera.'

patterns.title: Tener Expressions — 'To Have' = 'To Be'
patterns.text:
Spanish uses 'tener' (to have) where English uses 'to be':

• Tengo hambre = I'm hungry (I have hunger)
• Tengo 25 años = I'm 25 (I have 25 years)
• Tengo miedo = I'm scared (I have fear)
• Tiene razón = He's right (He has reason)
• Tengo sed = I'm thirsty (I have thirst)
• Tengo frío/calor = I'm cold/hot

lessons.title: Buenas
lessons.desc: Your very first words in Nicaragua

sn.s: Llego a Nicaragua.
sn.e: I arrive in Nicaragua.

sn.s: Hace calor.
sn.e: It's hot.

sn.s: Una señora me ve.
sn.e: A woman sees me.

sn.s: "¡Buenas!" me dice.
sn.e: "Hello!" she says to me.

sn.s: "Buenas," digo yo.
sn.e: "Hello," I say.

sn.s: Yo tengo sed.
sn.e: I'm thirsty. (lit: I have thirst.)

sn.s: "¿Agua, por favor?" digo.
sn.e: "Water, please?" I say.

sn.s: "Sí, claro," dice la señora.
sn.e: "Yes, of course," the woman says.

sn.s: Me da agua.
sn.e: She gives me water.

sn.s: "Gracias," digo yo.
sn.e: "Thank you," I say.

sn.s: "De nada," dice ella.
sn.e: "You're welcome," she says.

sn.s: El agua está bien fría.
sn.e: The water is nice and cold.

sn.s: Yo estoy bien.
sn.e: I am good.

sn.s: "Adiós, señora. Gracias."
sn.e: "Goodbye, ma'am. Thank you."

sn.s: "Adiós. Que le vaya bien," dice ella.
sn.e: "Goodbye. Take care," she says.

sn.s: Yo llegar a Managua por la noche.
sn.e: I arrive in Managua at night.

sn.s: Tengo mucho hambre.
sn.e: I'm very hungry.

sn.s: En la calle hay una fritanga.
sn.e: On the street there's a fritanga.

sn.s: La mujer se llama doña Carmen.
sn.e: The woman's name is doña Carmen.

sn.s: "¡Hola! ¿Qué querés comer?" me dice con una gran sonrisa.
sn.e: "Hi! What do you want to eat?" she says with a big smile.

sn.s: Yo no sé qué decir. Todo se ve muy bien.
sn.e: I don't know what to say. Everything looks really good.

sn.s: Hay gallo pinto, hay carne, hay tajadas de plátano, hay queso frito.
sn.e: There's gallo pinto, meat, plantain slices, and fried cheese.

sn.s: "Dale pues, te doy un poco de todo," dice ella.
sn.e: "Okay then, I'll give you a little of everything."

sn.s: La comida es muy buena. El gallo pinto tiene un sabor increíble.
sn.e: The food is really good. The gallo pinto has an incredible flavor.

sn.s: "¡Tuani!" dice ella. "Mañana tenés que venir otra vez."
sn.e: "Awesome!" she says. "Tomorrow you have to come again."

sn.s: La fritanga de doña Carmen es mi lugar favorito en Managua.
sn.e: Doña Carmen's fritanga is my favorite place in Managua.

sn.s: El mercado es grande. Hay mucha gente y mucho ruido.
sn.e: The market is big. Lots of people and noise.

sn.s: Yo necesito comprar comida para la casa.
sn.e: I need to buy food for the house.

sn.s: "Buenos días. ¿Cuánto por las naranjas?"
sn.e: "Good morning. How much for the oranges?"

sn.s: "Diez córdobas la bolsa," me dice.
sn.e: "Ten córdobas per bag," she tells me.

sn.s: "Pero si querés tres, te los dejo en doce."
sn.e: "But if you want three, I'll let them go for twelve."

sn.s: "Dale pues, me llevo tres mangos y una bolsa de naranjas."
sn.e: "Okay then, I'll take three mangos and a bag of oranges."

sn.s: Un hombre me dice: "Mirá, ahí donde ese chavalo está es donde venden el mejor arroz."
sn.e: "Look, where that kid is — that's where they sell the best rice."

sn.s: El chavalo es muy amable. "Aquí tenés. ¿Algo más?"
sn.e: The kid is very friendly. "Here you go. Anything else?"

sn.s: Le doy el dinero. "Gracias, que le vaya bien."
sn.e: I give him the money. "Thanks, take care."

sn.s: En el mercado siempre hay algo nuevo. Me gusta este lugar.
sn.e: At the market there's always something new. I like this place.

sn.s: Hay una pulpería cerca de mi casa. Cada tarde voy a comprar agua.
sn.e: There's a corner shop near my house. Every afternoon I buy water.

sn.s: Un día, un hombre me habla. "Vos no sos de aquí, ¿verdad?"
sn.e: One day, a man talks to me. "You're not from here, right?"

sn.s: "Soy de Estados Unidos." "¡Ideay! ¿Y qué hacés en Nicaragua?"
sn.e: "I'm from the US." "Well! What are you doing in Nicaragua?"

sn.s: "Quiero aprender español y conocer el país."
sn.e: "I want to learn Spanish and get to know the country."

sn.s: "Pues ya estás en el mejor lugar, hermano. Aquí la gente es tuani."
sn.e: "You're already in the best place, bro. People here are cool."

sn.s: "Mirá, yo soy Roberto. Si querés aprender como nica, tenés que salir con nosotros."
sn.e: "I'm Roberto. If you want to learn like a Nica, you have to hang with us."

sn.s: "No podés aprender solo en la casa con un libro."
sn.e: "You can't learn alone at home with a book."

sn.s: "Dale pues. Mañana en la noche vamos al parque."
sn.e: "Alright. Tomorrow night we're going to the park."

sn.s: Para aprender una lengua, tenés que vivir en ella. No solo estudiar. Vivir.
sn.e: To learn a language, you have to live in it. Not just study. Live.

sn.s: Necesito ir al otro lado de Managua. Paro un taxi en la calle.
sn.e: I need to cross Managua. I flag a taxi.

sn.s: "¿Para dónde vas?" me pregunta el chofer.
sn.e: "Where are you going?" asks the driver.

sn.s: "A la UCA, por favor." "Dale. ¿Sabés cuánto es?"
sn.e: "To the UCA, please." "Okay. Know how much?"

sn.s: "Cien córdobas." "¿No puede ser menos?" El chofer se ríe. "Ochenta."
sn.e: "A hundred córdobas." "Can't it be less?" He laughs. "Eighty."

sn.s: Vamos rápido por las calles de Managua.
sn.e: We go fast through the streets.

sn.s: "Mirá, eso es el lago de Managua," me dice.
sn.e: "Look, that's Lake Managua," he tells me.

sn.s: "Para llegar a tu casa desde la UCA: dos cuadras al norte, una cuadra arriba."
sn.e: "To get home from UCA: two blocks north, one block east."

sn.s: "Aquí arriba es al este, donde sale el sol. Abajo es al oeste."
sn.e: "Here 'arriba' is east, where the sun rises. 'Abajo' is west."

sn.s: Le doy los ochenta córdobas. "Gracias, que le vaya bien."
sn.e: I pay eighty córdobas. "Thanks, take care."

sn.s: Hoy no me siento bien. Me duele la cabeza y el estómago.
sn.e: I don't feel well. My head and stomach hurt.

sn.s: Creo que la comida de ayer me hizo mal.
sn.e: I think yesterday's food made me sick.

sn.s: Roberto viene. "¡Ideay! Te ves mal, hermano. ¿Qué te pasa?"
sn.e: Roberto comes. "Whoa! You look bad, bro. What's wrong?"

sn.s: "Estoy enfermo. Me duele todo el cuerpo."
sn.e: "I'm sick. My whole body hurts."

sn.s: "Mirá, aquí cerca hay una farmacia. Yo voy a comprar medicina para vos."
sn.e: "There's a pharmacy nearby. I'll buy medicine for you."

sn.s: Roberto vuelve con pastillas. "Tomá estas con agua. Una cada ocho horas."
sn.e: Roberto returns with pills. "Take these with water. One every eight hours."

sn.s: "Y tenés que descansar. Nada de salir hoy."
sn.e: "And you need to rest. No going out today."

sn.s: "Gracias, hermano. Sos muy amable." "Dale pues. Para eso son los amigos."
sn.e: "Thanks, bro." "No worries. That's what friends are for."

sn.s: Tomo la medicina y duermo todo el día. Al otro día me siento mucho mejor.
sn.e: I take the medicine and sleep all day. Next day I feel much better.

sn.s: Es sábado. Roberto me dice: "Hoy hay fiesta en el barrio. Tenés que venir."
sn.e: It's Saturday. Roberto: "There's a party tonight. You have to come."

sn.s: Llego a la fiesta. Hay música, comida, cerveza. Todos están contentos.
sn.e: I arrive. Music, food, beer. Everyone's happy.

sn.s: Roberto me presenta a su familia. "Esta es mi madre, doña Rosa."
sn.e: Roberto introduces his family. "This is my mother, doña Rosa."

sn.s: "Mucho gusto. Roberto es muy buen amigo," les digo.
sn.e: "Nice to meet you. Roberto is a great friend," I say.

sn.s: "¡Ideay! Vos sos el chele del que habla Roberto," dice doña Rosa.
sn.e: "So you're the foreigner Roberto talks about," says doña Rosa.

sn.s: "Bienvenido a nuestra casa. Aquí tenés tu casa también."
sn.e: "Welcome. This is your home too."

sn.s: La comida es increíble: nacatamales, vigorón, tajadas con queso.
sn.e: The food is incredible: nacatamales, vigorón, plantain chips with cheese.

sn.s: Karla me dice: "La mejor forma de aprender es así, con la gente."
sn.e: Karla tells me: "The best way to learn is like this, with people."

sn.s: Esta noche hablo más español que nunca. No es perfecto, pero la gente me entiende.
sn.e: Tonight I speak more Spanish than ever. Not perfect, but people understand me.

sn.s: Eso es lo que importa.
sn.e: That's what matters.

lessons.title: Mi primer trabajo
lessons.desc: Getting your first job in Nicaragua

sn.s: Ya tengo dos meses en Nicaragua. Mi dinero se está terminando.
sn.e: I've been in Nicaragua two months. My money is running out.

sn.s: Roberto me dice: "Mirá, mi amigo tiene un café y necesita a alguien que hable inglés."
sn.e: Roberto: "My friend has a café and needs someone who speaks English."

sn.s: "¿Para qué necesita inglés?" "Porque van muchos turistas."
sn.e: "Why does he need English?" "Because lots of tourists go there."

sn.s: Voy al café. El dueño se llama Marcos.
sn.e: I go to the café. The owner is Marcos.

sn.s: "¿Sabés hacer café?" me pregunta. "Sí, puedo aprender rápido."
sn.e: "Do you know how to make coffee?" "Yes, I can learn fast."

sn.s: "Dale. Empezás mañana. De lunes a viernes, ocho horas. Te pago por semana."
sn.e: "Okay. You start tomorrow. Monday to Friday, eight hours. I pay weekly."

sn.s: En el trabajo hablo español todo el día con los otros trabajadores.
sn.e: At work I speak Spanish all day with the other workers.

sn.s: Con los turistas hablo inglés, pero después cambio a español.
sn.e: With tourists I speak English, but then switch to Spanish.

sn.s: Mi español mejora cada semana. Ahora pienso en español sin traducir del inglés.
sn.e: My Spanish improves every week. Now I think in Spanish without translating.

lessons.title: La llamada de teléfono
lessons.desc: Your first phone call in Spanish

sn.s: Mi teléfono suena. Es un número que no conozco.
sn.e: My phone rings. A number I don't know.

sn.s: "¿Aló?" "Hola, ¿es Miguel? Soy Karla."
sn.e: "Hello?" "Hi, is this Miguel? It's Karla."

sn.s: "¡Karla! ¿Cómo estás?" "Bien, mirá, te llamo porque hay un problema."
sn.e: "Karla! How are you?" "Good, listen, I'm calling because there's a problem."

sn.s: "Roberto está enfermo y no puede ir al trabajo. ¿Podés decirle a Marcos?"
sn.e: "Roberto is sick and can't go to work. Can you tell Marcos?"

sn.s: Yo entiendo todo. Hace un mes no podía entender una llamada en español.
sn.e: I understand everything. A month ago I couldn't understand a phone call in Spanish.

sn.s: "Sí, claro. Yo le digo. ¿Necesita algo Roberto?"
sn.e: "Yes, of course. I'll tell him. Does Roberto need anything?"

sn.s: "No, solo descansar. Gracias, Miguel. Sos muy amable."
sn.e: "No, just rest. Thanks, Miguel. You're very kind."

sn.s: Después de la llamada, me siento bien. Puedo hablar por teléfono en español.
sn.e: After the call, I feel good. I can talk on the phone in Spanish.

sn.s: Eso es un gran paso. El teléfono es más difícil que hablar en persona.
sn.e: That's a big step. Phone is harder than in-person.

lessons.title: Perdido en Managua
lessons.desc: Getting lost and finding your way

sn.s: Hoy voy a un lugar nuevo en Managua. Pero me pierdo.
sn.e: Today I go somewhere new in Managua. But I get lost.

sn.s: No sé dónde estoy. Las calles no tienen nombre.
sn.e: I don't know where I am. The streets have no names.

sn.s: Le pregunto a una señora: "Disculpe, ¿sabe dónde está la Rotonda Santo Domingo?"
sn.e: I ask a woman: "Excuse me, do you know where the Santo Domingo roundabout is?"

sn.s: "Sí, mirá. Vas derecho dos cuadras, después a la izquierda en la esquina."
sn.e: "Yes, look. Go straight two blocks, then left at the corner."

sn.s: "Después seguís tres cuadras más al norte, y ahí la ves."
sn.e: "Then continue three more blocks north, and you'll see it."

sn.s: Sigo sus instrucciones. Derecho, izquierda, norte.
sn.e: I follow her directions. Straight, left, north.

sn.s: Pero me pierdo otra vez. Le pregunto a un chavalo.
sn.e: But I get lost again. I ask a kid.

sn.s: "¿La Rotonda? Está cerquita. Mirá, yo voy para allá. Vení conmigo."
sn.e: "The roundabout? It's close. Look, I'm going there. Come with me."

sn.s: Caminamos juntos. Me cuenta sobre su escuela y su familia.
sn.e: We walk together. He tells me about his school and family.

sn.s: Llego a la Rotonda. Perderme fue la mejor cosa del día.
sn.e: I reach the roundabout. Getting lost was the best thing today.

sn.s: Es octubre, la temporada de lluvia en Nicaragua.
sn.e: It's October, rainy season in Nicaragua.

sn.s: Una tarde el cielo se pone oscuro muy rápido.
sn.e: One afternoon the sky gets dark very fast.

sn.s: Empieza a llover. Pero no es lluvia normal. Es una tormenta fuerte.
sn.e: It starts to rain. Not normal rain. A strong storm.

sn.s: El agua entra por abajo de la puerta. Cierro las ventanas.
sn.e: Water comes under the door. I close the windows.

sn.s: La luz se va. Toda la casa está oscura.
sn.e: The power goes out. The whole house is dark.

sn.s: Roberto viene a mi puerta. "¿Estás bien? Vení a mi casa. Es más segura."
sn.e: Roberto comes to my door. "You okay? Come to my house. It's safer."

sn.s: Voy con Roberto. Su familia está en la sala con velas.
sn.e: I go with Roberto. His family is in the living room with candles.

sn.s: Doña Rosa me da café caliente. "No te preocupés. Esto pasa cada año."
sn.e: Doña Rosa gives me hot coffee. "Don't worry. This happens every year."

sn.s: Esperamos juntos. La familia habla, ríe, cuenta historias.
sn.e: We wait together. The family talks, laughs, tells stories.

sn.s: La tormenta es fuerte, pero adentro me siento seguro. Tengo una segunda familia aquí.
sn.e: The storm is strong, but inside I feel safe. I have a second family here.

sn.s: Marcos, el dueño del café, quiere cambiar mi horario de trabajo.
sn.e: Marcos, the café owner, wants to change my work schedule.

sn.s: "Miguel, necesito que trabajés los sábados también."
sn.e: "Miguel, I need you to work Saturdays too."

sn.s: "Pero los sábados yo estudio español con un profesor."
sn.e: "But Saturdays I study Spanish with a teacher."

sn.s: "Lo siento, pero necesito a alguien los sábados. Es el día más ocupado."
sn.e: "Sorry, but I need someone on Saturdays. It's the busiest day."

sn.s: "Marcos, yo creo que eso no es justo. No estaba en nuestro acuerdo."
sn.e: "Marcos, I don't think that's fair. It wasn't in our agreement."

sn.s: Marcos se queda callado un momento. Yo pienso que se va a enojar.
sn.e: Marcos goes quiet. I think he's going to get angry.

sn.s: "Tenés razón," dice. "No estaba en el acuerdo. Mirá, ¿qué te parece si trabajás solo medio día el sábado?"
sn.e: "You're right," he says. "It wasn't in the deal. How about half a day Saturday?"

sn.s: "Dale, eso sí puedo hacer."
sn.e: "Okay, I can do that."

sn.s: Es la primera vez que tengo una discusión seria en español. Y la gané.
sn.e: It's my first serious argument in Spanish. And I won.

sn.s: No solo puedo hablar español. Puedo defenderme en español.
sn.e: I can't just speak Spanish. I can defend myself in Spanish.

sn.s: Hoy se cumplen seis meses desde que llegué a Nicaragua.
sn.e: Today marks six months since I arrived in Nicaragua.

sn.s: Pienso en el primer día, cuando no sabía nada de español.
sn.e: I think about day one, when I knew no Spanish.

sn.s: Ahora puedo ir al mercado y regatear. Puedo tomar un taxi sin problema.
sn.e: Now I can go to the market and haggle. Take a taxi, no problem.

sn.s: Puedo hacer amigos, contar chistes, y hasta discutir en español.
sn.e: I can make friends, tell jokes, even argue in Spanish.

sn.s: Todavía cometo errores. A veces busco una palabra y no la encuentro.
sn.e: I still make mistakes. Sometimes I search for a word and can't find it.

sn.s: Pero ya no tengo miedo de hablar. Ese es el cambio más grande.
sn.e: But I'm no longer afraid to speak. That's the biggest change.

sn.s: Roberto me dice: "Hermano, ya hablás como nica."
sn.e: Roberto tells me: "Bro, you already talk like a Nica."

sn.s: No es verdad todavía. Pero cada día estoy más cerca.
sn.e: It's not true yet. But every day I'm closer.

sn.s: La fluidez no es saber todas las palabras. Es poder vivir tu vida en otro idioma.
sn.e: Fluency isn't knowing every word. It's being able to live your life in another language.

sn.s: Y eso es lo que estoy haciendo.
sn.e: And that's what I'm doing.

sn.s: Quiero comprar fruta.
sn.e: I want to buy fruit.

sn.s: Hay una mesa con mangos y naranjas.
sn.e: There's a table with mangos and oranges.

sn.s: Una mujer vende la fruta.
sn.e: A woman sells the fruit.

sn.s: "Buenas. ¿Cuánto cuesta un mango?"
sn.e: "Hello. How much is a mango?"

sn.s: "Cinco córdobas," dice ella.
sn.e: "Five córdobas," she says.

sn.s: "¿Y tres mangos?"
sn.e: "And three mangos?"

sn.s: "Tres mangos, diez córdobas."
sn.e: "Three mangos, ten córdobas."

sn.s: Ah, tres por diez es mejor.
sn.e: Ah, three for ten is better.

sn.s: "Dale. Tres mangos, por favor."
sn.e: "Okay. Three mangos, please."

sn.s: "¿Algo más?" dice la mujer.
sn.e: "Anything else?" the woman says.

sn.s: "Dos naranjas también."
sn.e: "Two oranges too."

sn.s: "Son quince córdobas en total."
sn.e: "That's fifteen córdobas total."

sn.s: Le doy el dinero.
sn.e: I give her the money.

sn.s: Ahora sé los números. Uno, dos, tres...
sn.e: Now I know the numbers. One, two, three...

sn.s: Los números son la llave del mercado.
sn.e: Numbers are the key to the market.

sn.s: En el mercado todo se puede regatear.
sn.e: At the market you can haggle for everything.

sn.s: Veo una camisa bonita.
sn.e: I see a nice shirt.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto cuesta esta camisa?"
sn.e: "How much is this shirt?"

sn.s: "Doscientos córdobas," dice el hombre.
sn.e: "Two hundred córdobas," the man says.

sn.s: Es un poco caro para mí.
sn.e: It's a little expensive for me.

sn.s: "Está caro. ¿No hay rebaja?"
sn.e: "That's expensive. No discount?"

sn.s: El hombre piensa un momento.
sn.e: The man thinks for a moment.

sn.s: "Para vos, ciento cincuenta."
sn.e: "For you, a hundred fifty."

sn.s: "¿Ciento veinte?" digo yo.
sn.e: "A hundred twenty?" I say.

sn.s: "Ciento treinta y te la llevás."
sn.e: "A hundred thirty and you take it."

sn.s: "Dale pues. Ciento treinta."
sn.e: "Okay then. A hundred thirty."

sn.s: El hombre pone la camisa en una bolsa.
sn.e: The man puts the shirt in a bag.

sn.s: "Gracias, chele. Que le vaya bien."
sn.e: "Thanks, foreigner. Take care."

sn.s: Regatear no es pelear. Es parte del juego.
sn.e: Haggling isn't fighting. It's part of the game.

sn.s: Y a la gente le gusta cuando vos lo intentás.
sn.e: And people like it when you give it a try.

lessons.title: En la pulpería
lessons.desc: The corner store and daily ritual

sn.s: Cerca de mi casa hay una pulpería.
sn.e: Near my house there's a corner store.

sn.s: La dueña es doña Marta.
sn.e: The owner is doña Marta.

sn.s: Voy todos los días.
sn.e: I go every day.

sn.s: "Buenas, doña Marta. ¿Cómo está?"
sn.e: "Hello, doña Marta. How are you?"

sn.s: "Bien, gracias a Dios. ¿Y vos?"
sn.e: "Good, thank God. And you?"

sn.s: "Bien. Quiero pan y dos huevos."
sn.e: "Good. I want bread and two eggs."

sn.s: Doña Marta conoce a todos los vecinos.
sn.e: Doña Marta knows all the neighbors.

sn.s: Un señor llega. "Doña Marta, ¿me fía hasta el viernes?"
sn.e: "Doña Marta, can you let me pay on Friday?"

sn.s: "Claro, don Beto. Como siempre."
sn.e: "Of course, don Beto. Like always."

sn.s: Aquí la gente compra fiado y paga después.
sn.e: Here people buy on credit and pay later.

sn.s: Es confianza entre vecinos.
sn.e: It's trust between neighbors.

sn.s: "Aquí tenés tu pan," me dice doña Marta.
sn.e: "Here's your bread," doña Marta tells me.

sn.s: "Gracias. Hasta mañana."
sn.e: "Thanks. See you tomorrow."

sn.s: La pulpería no es solo una tienda.
sn.e: The corner store isn't just a shop.

sn.s: Es el corazón del barrio.
sn.e: It's the heart of the neighborhood.

sn.s: Busco la casa de un amigo.
sn.e: I'm looking for a friend's house.

sn.s: Pero en Managua las calles no tienen nombre.
sn.e: But in Managua the streets have no names.

sn.s: Le pregunto a una señora.
sn.e: I ask a woman.

sn.s: "Disculpe, ¿dónde está la casa azul?"
sn.e: "Excuse me, where is the blue house?"

sn.s: "¿Cuál casa, mi amor?"
sn.e: "Which house, dear?"

sn.s: "La que está cerca del parque."
sn.e: "The one near the park."

sn.s: "Ah, ya sé. Mirá: de la iglesia, dos cuadras arriba."
sn.e: "Ah, I know. Look: from the church, two blocks east."

sn.s: "¿Arriba es para allá?" pregunto.
sn.e: "Is 'arriba' that way?" I ask.

sn.s: "Sí, arriba es donde sale el sol. El este."
sn.e: "Yes, 'arriba' is where the sun rises. The east."

sn.s: "Después una cuadra al sur, en la esquina."
sn.e: "Then one block south, on the corner."

sn.s: Aquí no usan norte y sur como yo.
sn.e: Here they don't use north and south like I do.

sn.s: Usan el lago, el sol, y los lugares conocidos.
sn.e: They use the lake, the sun, and known places.

sn.s: "Muchas gracias, señora."
sn.e: "Thank you very much, ma'am."

sn.s: "De nada. Que Dios te acompañe."
sn.e: "You're welcome. May God go with you."

sn.s: Encuentro la casa azul. ¡Lo logré!
sn.e: I find the blue house. I did it!

sn.s: Necesito ir al centro.
sn.e: I need to go downtown.

sn.s: Tomo el bus en la parada.
sn.e: I take the bus at the stop.

sn.s: El bus llega lleno de gente.
sn.e: The bus arrives full of people.

sn.s: Subo con cuidado.
sn.e: I get on carefully.

sn.s: "¡Pasaje, pasaje!" grita el cobrador.
sn.e: "Fare, fare!" shouts the fare collector.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto es el pasaje?" pregunto.
sn.e: "How much is the fare?" I ask.

sn.s: "Cinco córdobas," me dice.
sn.e: "Five córdobas," he tells me.

sn.s: Le doy el dinero.
sn.e: I give him the money.

sn.s: No hay asiento. Voy de pie.
sn.e: There's no seat. I stand.

sn.s: El bus va rápido por la ciudad.
sn.e: The bus goes fast through the city.

sn.s: Una señora me dice: "Agárrese bien, joven."
sn.e: A woman tells me: "Hold on tight, young man."

sn.s: "¡Parada!" grito cuando llego.
sn.e: "Stop!" I shout when I arrive.

sn.s: Bajo del bus en el centro.
sn.e: I get off the bus downtown.

sn.s: El bus es caótico, pero funciona.
sn.e: The bus is chaotic, but it works.

sn.s: Y siempre hay alguien que te ayuda.
sn.e: And there's always someone who helps you.

sn.s: Es hora del almuerzo.
sn.e: It's lunchtime.

sn.s: Entro a un comedor pequeño.
sn.e: I go into a small eatery.

sn.s: "Buenas. ¿Qué hay de almuerzo?"
sn.e: "Hello. What's for lunch?"

sn.s: "Hay carne asada con gallo pinto, maduro y cuajada."
sn.e: "There's grilled meat with gallo pinto, fried plantain, and cuajada cheese."

sn.s: "Suena rico. Quiero eso, por favor."
sn.e: "Sounds delicious. I want that, please."

sn.s: "¿Y de tomar?"
sn.e: "And to drink?"

sn.s: "¿Qué refrescos tienen?"
sn.e: "What drinks do you have?"

sn.s: "De cacao, de tamarindo, de chía."
sn.e: "Cacao, tamarind, chia."

sn.s: "Un refresco de cacao, por favor."
sn.e: "A cacao drink, please."

sn.s: La comida llega. Todo se ve increíble.
sn.e: The food arrives. Everything looks incredible.

sn.s: El gallo pinto es el alma de Nicaragua.
sn.e: Gallo pinto is the soul of Nicaragua.

sn.s: Arroz, frijoles, y mucho sabor.
sn.e: Rice, beans, and lots of flavor.

sn.s: Como hasta quedar lleno.
sn.e: I eat until I'm full.

sn.s: "¿Le gustó?" pregunta la señora.
sn.e: "Did you like it?" the woman asks.

sn.s: "Me encantó. Estaba bien rico."
sn.e: "I loved it. It was really delicious."

lessons.title: El teléfono
lessons.desc: Getting a SIM card and going online

sn.s: Mi teléfono no tiene internet.
sn.e: My phone has no internet.

sn.s: Necesito un chip de aquí.
sn.e: I need a local SIM card.

sn.s: Voy a una tienda de teléfonos.
sn.e: I go to a phone store.

sn.s: "Buenas. Necesito un chip nuevo."
sn.e: "Hello. I need a new SIM card."

sn.s: "¿Para llamadas o para internet?"
sn.e: "For calls or for internet?"

sn.s: "Para los dos, por favor."
sn.e: "For both, please."

sn.s: El joven pone el chip en mi teléfono.
sn.e: The young man puts the SIM in my phone.

sn.s: "Listo. Este es tu número nuevo."
sn.e: "Done. This is your new number."

sn.s: "¿Cómo recargo el saldo?" pregunto.
sn.e: "How do I add credit?" I ask.

sn.s: "En cualquier pulpería. Decís tu número y pagás."
sn.e: "At any corner store. You say your number and pay."

sn.s: "¿Cuánto para un mes de internet?"
sn.e: "How much for a month of internet?"

sn.s: "Doscientos córdobas y te dura el mes."
sn.e: "Two hundred córdobas and it lasts the month."

sn.s: Ahora puedo llamar y mandar mensajes.
sn.e: Now I can call and send messages.

sn.s: Le mando un mensaje a Roberto.
sn.e: I send Roberto a message.

sn.s: "Ya tengo número nica," le escribo.
sn.e: "I have a Nica number now," I write him.

sn.s: Roberto me llama por teléfono.
sn.e: Roberto calls me on the phone.

sn.s: "¿Qué hacés el sábado?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "What are you doing Saturday?" he asks me.

sn.s: "Nada todavía. ¿Por qué?"
sn.e: "Nothing yet. Why?"

sn.s: "Vamos a la playa con unos amigos."
sn.e: "We're going to the beach with some friends."

sn.s: "¡Dale! Me encanta la idea."
sn.e: "Yes! I love the idea."

sn.s: "¿A qué hora salimos?" pregunto.
sn.e: "What time do we leave?" I ask.

sn.s: "Temprano. Como a las seis de la mañana."
sn.e: "Early. Around six in the morning."

sn.s: "¿Tan temprano?" digo yo.
sn.e: "That early?" I say.

sn.s: "Sí, para llegar antes del calor."
sn.e: "Yes, to arrive before the heat."

sn.s: "¿Dónde nos quedamos de ver?"
sn.e: "Where do we meet up?"

sn.s: "En mi casa. No llegués tarde."
sn.e: "At my house. Don't be late."

sn.s: "Tranquilo. Voy a estar ahí temprano."
sn.e: "Relax. I'll be there early."

sn.s: "Perfecto. Nos vemos el sábado."
sn.e: "Perfect. See you Saturday."

sn.s: Tengo planes con amigos nicas.
sn.e: I have plans with Nica friends.

sn.s: Eso sí es sentirse en casa.
sn.e: That really is feeling at home.

lessons.title: Un problema pequeño
lessons.desc: Dealing with a small daily problem

sn.s: Hoy tengo un problema.
sn.e: Today I have a problem.

sn.s: La llave no abre la puerta.
sn.e: The key won't open the door.

sn.s: La cerradura está rota.
sn.e: The lock is broken.

sn.s: No puedo entrar a mi casa.
sn.e: I can't get into my house.

sn.s: Mi vecino me ve afuera.
sn.e: My neighbor sees me outside.

sn.s: "¿Qué pasó, vecino?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "What happened, neighbor?" he asks me.

sn.s: "La cerradura está rota. No puedo entrar."
sn.e: "The lock is broken. I can't get in."

sn.s: "Esperá, yo te ayudo."
sn.e: "Wait, I'll help you."

sn.s: El vecino conoce a un cerrajero.
sn.e: The neighbor knows a locksmith.

sn.s: "Don Chico arregla todo. Yo lo llamo."
sn.e: "Don Chico fixes everything. I'll call him."

sn.s: En media hora llega don Chico.
sn.e: In half an hour don Chico arrives.

sn.s: Arregla la cerradura rápido.
sn.e: He fixes the lock quickly.

sn.s: "Ya está. Quedó como nueva."
sn.e: "All done. Good as new."

sn.s: "Muchas gracias a los dos."
sn.e: "Thank you both very much."

sn.s: Aquí los vecinos se ayudan. Siempre.
sn.e: Here neighbors help each other. Always.

sn.s: En Nicaragua hay dos estaciones.
sn.e: In Nicaragua there are two seasons.

sn.s: El verano seco y el invierno con lluvia.
sn.e: The dry summer and the rainy winter.

sn.s: Hoy el cielo está lleno de nubes.
sn.e: Today the sky is full of clouds.

sn.s: Camino por la calle sin paraguas.
sn.e: I walk down the street without an umbrella.

sn.s: De repente empieza a llover.
sn.e: Suddenly it starts to rain.

sn.s: La lluvia es muy fuerte.
sn.e: The rain is very heavy.

sn.s: Me meto en una pulpería.
sn.e: I duck into a corner store.

sn.s: "Esta lluvia no avisa," dice la dueña riendo.
sn.e: "This rain gives no warning," the owner says, laughing.

sn.s: "¿Dura mucho?" pregunto.
sn.e: "Does it last long?" I ask.

sn.s: "No, un rato. Después sale el sol."
sn.e: "No, a while. Then the sun comes out."

sn.s: Espero adentro con un café.
sn.e: I wait inside with a coffee.

sn.s: En veinte minutos la lluvia para.
sn.e: In twenty minutes the rain stops.

sn.s: El sol sale otra vez.
sn.e: The sun comes out again.

sn.s: Todo huele a tierra mojada.
sn.e: Everything smells of wet earth.

sn.s: Así es el invierno nica: fuerte y rápido.
sn.e: That's the Nica winter: strong and fast.

sn.s: Roberto quiere saber más de mí.
sn.e: Roberto wants to know more about me.

sn.s: "Contame de tu vida," me dice.
sn.e: "Tell me about your life," he says.

sn.s: "Bueno, tengo treinta años."
sn.e: "Well, I'm thirty years old."

sn.s: "Soy soltero, no tengo hijos."
sn.e: "I'm single, I have no kids."

sn.s: "¿Y tu familia?" pregunta él.
sn.e: "And your family?" he asks.

sn.s: "Tengo dos hermanos y una hermana."
sn.e: "I have two brothers and one sister."

sn.s: "Ellos viven en los Estados Unidos."
sn.e: "They live in the United States."

sn.s: "¿En qué trabajás?"
sn.e: "What do you do for work?"

sn.s: "Trabajo con computadoras. Soy programador."
sn.e: "I work with computers. I'm a programmer."

sn.s: "¡Qué bueno! ¿Y te gusta vivir aquí?"
sn.e: "How nice! And do you like living here?"

sn.s: "Me encanta. La gente es muy cálida."
sn.e: "I love it. The people are very warm."

sn.s: "Aquí ya tenés familia también," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Here you have family too now," says Roberto.

sn.s: Sus palabras me llegan al corazón.
sn.e: His words touch my heart.

sn.s: Hablar de mi vida en español ya no me da miedo.
sn.e: Talking about my life in Spanish no longer scares me.

lessons.title: El fin de semana
lessons.desc: What you did over the weekend

sn.s: Es lunes. Roberto me pregunta por mi fin de semana.
sn.e: It's Monday. Roberto asks about my weekend.

sn.s: "¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana?"
sn.e: "What did you do over the weekend?"

sn.s: Quiero contarle, pero en pasado.
sn.e: I want to tell him, but in the past tense.

sn.s: "El sábado fui a la playa," digo.
sn.e: "On Saturday I went to the beach," I say.

sn.s: "¿Y qué tal estuvo?"
sn.e: "And how was it?"

sn.s: "Estuvo muy divertido. Nadé en el mar."
sn.e: "It was a lot of fun. I swam in the sea."

sn.s: "Comí pescado fresco con unos amigos."
sn.e: "I ate fresh fish with some friends."

sn.s: "¡Qué rico! ¿Y el domingo?"
sn.e: "How delicious! And Sunday?"

sn.s: "El domingo descansé en casa."
sn.e: "On Sunday I rested at home."

sn.s: "Vi una película y dormí mucho."
sn.e: "I watched a movie and slept a lot."

sn.s: Hablar del pasado es difícil, pero lo intento.
sn.e: Talking about the past is hard, but I try.

sn.s: "Hablás cada vez mejor," me dice Roberto.
sn.e: "You speak better and better," Roberto tells me.

sn.s: Fui, comí, vi, dormí. El pasado tiene su ritmo.
sn.e: I went, I ate, I saw, I slept. The past has its rhythm.

sn.s: Poco a poco, cuento mis propias historias.
sn.e: Little by little, I tell my own stories.

sn.s: Roberto me invita a cenar a su casa.
sn.e: Roberto invites me to dinner at his house.

sn.s: "Mi mamá quiere conocerte," me dice.
sn.e: "My mom wants to meet you," he says.

sn.s: Llego con un poco de nervios.
sn.e: I arrive a little nervous.

sn.s: "¡Pase, pase! Bienvenido," dice su mamá.
sn.e: "Come in, come in! Welcome," says his mom.

sn.s: "Buenas noches, doña. Gracias por invitarme."
sn.e: "Good evening, ma'am. Thank you for inviting me."

sn.s: "Siéntese. Está en su casa."
sn.e: "Sit down. Make yourself at home."

sn.s: La mesa está llena de comida.
sn.e: The table is full of food.

sn.s: "Hice gallo pinto y pollo. Coma, coma."
sn.e: "I made gallo pinto and chicken. Eat, eat."

sn.s: "Todo está riquísimo, doña. Gracias."
sn.e: "Everything is delicious, ma'am. Thank you."

sn.s: Platicamos toda la noche.
sn.e: We chat all night.

sn.s: Me preguntan de mi familia, de mi país.
sn.e: They ask about my family, my country.

sn.s: "Aquí siempre tenés un plato en esta mesa," dice ella.
sn.e: "Here you always have a plate at this table," she says.

sn.s: Me siento parte de algo.
sn.e: I feel like part of something.

sn.s: En Nicaragua, invitarte a comer es abrirte el corazón.
sn.e: In Nicaragua, inviting you to eat is opening their heart to you.

sn.s: La mamá de Roberto quiere saber de mi país.
sn.e: Roberto's mom wants to know about my country.

sn.s: "¿Cómo es tu pueblo?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "What's your town like?" she asks me.

sn.s: "Es muy diferente de aquí," le digo.
sn.e: "It's very different from here," I tell her.

sn.s: "Allá hace frío en el invierno."
sn.e: "There it's cold in the winter."

sn.s: "¿Frío de verdad? ¿Con nieve?"
sn.e: "Real cold? With snow?"

sn.s: "Sí, a veces cae nieve."
sn.e: "Yes, sometimes snow falls."

sn.s: "¡Ay, no! Yo me muero de frío," dice riendo.
sn.e: "Oh, no! I'd die of cold," she says, laughing.

sn.s: "Mi pueblo es pequeño y tranquilo."
sn.e: "My town is small and quiet."

sn.s: "Hay montañas y muchos árboles."
sn.e: "There are mountains and many trees."

sn.s: "¿Y no extrañás tu casa?"
sn.e: "And don't you miss your home?"

sn.s: "A veces sí. Pero aquí encontré otra casa."
sn.e: "Sometimes yes. But here I found another home."

sn.s: "Los dos lugares son parte de mí ahora."
sn.e: "Both places are part of me now."

sn.s: Comparar mi mundo con el de ellos nos acerca.
sn.e: Comparing my world with theirs brings us closer.

sn.s: Hablar de dónde venís es compartir quién sos.
sn.e: Talking about where you're from is sharing who you are.

sn.s: En la cena, hablamos de lo que nos gusta.
sn.e: At dinner, we talk about what we like.

sn.s: "¿Qué hacés en tu tiempo libre?" pregunta Roberto.
sn.e: "What do you do in your free time?" Roberto asks.

sn.s: "Me gusta leer y caminar," digo.
sn.e: "I like to read and walk," I say.

sn.s: "¿Y la música? ¿Qué te gusta?"
sn.e: "And music? What do you like?"

sn.s: "Me gusta todo tipo de música."
sn.e: "I like all kinds of music."

sn.s: "¿Sabés bailar?" pregunta su hermana.
sn.e: "Do you know how to dance?" his sister asks.

sn.s: "Un poco, pero soy malo," digo riendo.
sn.e: "A little, but I'm bad," I say, laughing.

sn.s: "¡Aquí todos bailamos! Te enseñamos."
sn.e: "Here we all dance! We'll teach you."

sn.s: Ponen música y todos se levantan.
sn.e: They put on music and everyone gets up.

sn.s: "¿Te gusta el baile?" me pregunta ella.
sn.e: "Do you like dancing?" she asks me.

sn.s: "Ahora sí me encanta," respondo.
sn.e: "Now I really love it," I answer.

sn.s: Aprendo que 'me gusta' me abre muchas puertas.
sn.e: I learn that 'I like' opens many doors for me.

sn.s: Compartir lo que amás es hacer amigos.
sn.e: Sharing what you love is making friends.

sn.s: Esa noche bailo mal, pero río mucho.
sn.e: That night I dance badly, but I laugh a lot.

sn.s: Roberto me cuenta de su infancia.
sn.e: Roberto tells me about his childhood.

sn.s: "Cuando era niño, jugaba en la calle todo el día."
sn.e: "When I was a kid, I played in the street all day."

sn.s: "Mi abuela me cuidaba," dice con cariño.
sn.e: "My grandma took care of me," he says fondly.

sn.s: "¿Y vos? ¿Cómo eras de niño?"
sn.e: "And you? What were you like as a kid?"

sn.s: Pienso en el pasado. Esto es más difícil.
sn.e: I think about the past. This is harder.

sn.s: "Yo era tímido," digo despacio.
sn.e: "I was shy," I say slowly.

sn.s: "Siempre leía libros. No me gustaban los deportes."
sn.e: "I always read books. I didn't like sports."

sn.s: "Mi abuelo me contaba historias."
sn.e: "My grandpa used to tell me stories."

sn.s: "Esas historias me hicieron amar las palabras."
sn.e: "Those stories made me love words."

sn.s: "Por eso ahora aprendés idiomas," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "That's why you learn languages now," says Roberto.

sn.s: "Tal vez sí," respondo, sorprendido.
sn.e: "Maybe so," I answer, surprised.

sn.s: El imperfecto: era, jugaba, leía, contaba.
sn.e: The imperfect tense: I was, I played, I read, he told.

sn.s: Es el tiempo de los recuerdos.
sn.e: It's the tense of memories.

sn.s: Hablar de antes me ayuda a entender el ahora.
sn.e: Talking about before helps me understand the now.

sn.s: Hoy tuve un día terrible.
sn.e: Today I had a terrible day.

sn.s: Roberto nota que estoy molesto.
sn.e: Roberto notices I'm upset.

sn.s: "¿Qué te pasa? Te ves cansado."
sn.e: "What's wrong? You look tired."

sn.s: "Tuve un mal día," suspiro.
sn.e: "I had a bad day," I sigh.

sn.s: "Contame. Te escucho."
sn.e: "Tell me. I'm listening."

sn.s: "Perdí mi teléfono y llegué tarde al trabajo."
sn.e: "I lost my phone and arrived late to work."

sn.s: "Después olvidé una reunión importante."
sn.e: "Then I forgot an important meeting."

sn.s: "Uy, qué mala suerte," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Oof, what bad luck," says Roberto.

sn.s: "Me siento frustrado y un poco triste."
sn.e: "I feel frustrated and a little sad."

sn.s: "Tranquilo. Todos tenemos días así."
sn.e: "Relax. We all have days like this."

sn.s: "Mañana va a estar mejor. Ya verás."
sn.e: "Tomorrow will be better. You'll see."

sn.s: Hablar de lo que siento me quita un peso.
sn.e: Talking about what I feel takes a weight off me.

sn.s: "Gracias por escucharme," le digo.
sn.e: "Thanks for listening to me," I tell him.

sn.s: Un buen amigo y un poco de español: eso ayuda.
sn.e: A good friend and a little Spanish: that helps.

sn.s: Queremos hacer algo el sábado.
sn.e: We want to do something on Saturday.

sn.s: "¿Qué te parece ir al lago?" propone Roberto.
sn.e: "What do you think about going to the lake?" Roberto suggests.

sn.s: "Buena idea, pero hace mucho calor allá."
sn.e: "Good idea, but it's very hot there."

sn.s: "Tenés razón. ¿Qué preferís hacer?"
sn.e: "You're right. What do you prefer to do?"

sn.s: "Tal vez podríamos ir a las montañas."
sn.e: "Maybe we could go to the mountains."

sn.s: "Allá hace más fresco," agrego.
sn.e: "It's cooler there," I add.

sn.s: "Me gusta la idea. Pero está lejos."
sn.e: "I like the idea. But it's far."

sn.s: "¿Y si vamos el domingo entonces?"
sn.e: "What if we go on Sunday then?"

sn.s: "Perfecto. Así tenemos todo el día."
sn.e: "Perfect. That way we have the whole day."

sn.s: "Estoy de acuerdo," digo contento.
sn.e: "I agree," I say happily.

sn.s: No siempre pensamos igual, y está bien.
sn.e: We don't always think alike, and that's okay.

sn.s: Aprendí a decir 'no estoy de acuerdo' sin pelear.
sn.e: I learned to say 'I disagree' without fighting.

sn.s: Proponer, escuchar, decidir juntos.
sn.e: Suggesting, listening, deciding together.

sn.s: Así se construye una amistad de verdad.
sn.e: That's how a real friendship is built.

sn.s: Roberto y yo hablamos de política.
sn.e: Roberto and I talk about politics.

sn.s: "Yo creo que la ciudad necesita más buses," dice él.
sn.e: "I think the city needs more buses," he says.

sn.s: "Entiendo tu punto, pero no estoy de acuerdo."
sn.e: "I understand your point, but I disagree."

sn.s: "¿Por qué no?" pregunta, curioso.
sn.e: "Why not?" he asks, curious.

sn.s: "Creo que el problema no son los buses."
sn.e: "I think the problem isn't the buses."

sn.s: "El problema son las calles, que están malas."
sn.e: "The problem is the streets, which are bad."

sn.s: "Tenés razón en eso," admite Roberto.
sn.e: "You're right about that," Roberto admits.

sn.s: "Aunque pienso que las dos cosas importan."
sn.e: "Although I think both things matter."

sn.s: "Es verdad. Tal vez los dos tenemos razón."
sn.e: "That's true. Maybe we're both right."

sn.s: Discutir sin pelear es un arte.
sn.e: Arguing without fighting is an art.

sn.s: Aprendí a decir 'no estoy de acuerdo' con respeto.
sn.e: I learned to say 'I disagree' with respect.

sn.s: Se puede diferir y seguir siendo amigos.
sn.e: You can differ and still be friends.

sn.s: Defender una idea en español me da confianza.
sn.e: Defending an idea in Spanish gives me confidence.

sn.s: Ya no solo escucho: ahora participo.
sn.e: I no longer just listen: now I take part.

sn.s: Compré un ventilador la semana pasada.
sn.e: I bought a fan last week.

sn.s: Pero ya no funciona. Está roto.
sn.e: But it doesn't work anymore. It's broken.

sn.s: Vuelvo a la tienda con el recibo.
sn.e: I go back to the store with the receipt.

sn.s: "Buenas. Compré este ventilador y ya no sirve."
sn.e: "Hello. I bought this fan and it no longer works."

sn.s: "¿Tiene el recibo?" pregunta la empleada.
sn.e: "Do you have the receipt?" the employee asks.

sn.s: "Sí, aquí está. Lo compré hace una semana."
sn.e: "Yes, here it is. I bought it a week ago."

sn.s: "Quiero un cambio o que me devuelvan el dinero."
sn.e: "I want an exchange or my money back."

sn.s: "Déjeme revisar la garantía," dice ella.
sn.e: "Let me check the warranty," she says.

sn.s: Hablo con calma, pero soy firme.
sn.e: I speak calmly, but I'm firm.

sn.s: "Creo que es un reclamo razonable," agrego.
sn.e: "I think it's a reasonable complaint," I add.

sn.s: "Tiene razón. Le damos uno nuevo."
sn.e: "You're right. We'll give you a new one."

sn.s: "Se lo agradezco mucho," respondo.
sn.e: "I appreciate it very much," I respond.

sn.s: Reclamar bien no es ser grosero.
sn.e: Complaining well isn't being rude.

sn.s: Es defender lo que es justo, con respeto.
sn.e: It's standing up for what's fair, with respect.

sn.s: Necesito abrir una cuenta en el banco.
sn.e: I need to open a bank account.

sn.s: Hago una larga fila para esperar.
sn.e: I wait in a long line.

sn.s: "Buenos días. Quiero abrir una cuenta," digo.
sn.e: "Good morning. I'd like to open an account," I say.

sn.s: "¿Trae su cédula o pasaporte?" pregunta el cajero.
sn.e: "Do you have your ID or passport?" the teller asks.

sn.s: "Sí, traigo mi pasaporte."
sn.e: "Yes, I have my passport."

sn.s: "¿Cuáles son los otros requisitos?" pregunto.
sn.e: "What are the other requirements?" I ask.

sn.s: "Necesita llenar este formulario y firmar aquí."
sn.e: "You need to fill out this form and sign here."

sn.s: El trámite tiene muchos papeles.
sn.e: The process has a lot of paperwork.

sn.s: "¿Dónde firmo exactamente?" pregunto, con cuidado.
sn.e: "Where exactly do I sign?" I ask, carefully.

sn.s: "Aquí abajo, y ponga la fecha."
sn.e: "Down here, and put the date."

sn.s: Firmo cada documento despacio.
sn.e: I sign each document slowly.

sn.s: "Listo. Su cuenta estará activa mañana."
sn.e: "Done. Your account will be active tomorrow."

sn.s: Los trámites en español ya no me asustan.
sn.e: Paperwork in Spanish no longer scares me.

sn.s: Preguntar con calma resuelve casi todo.
sn.e: Asking calmly solves almost everything.

sn.s: Roberto parece molesto conmigo hoy.
sn.e: Roberto seems upset with me today.

sn.s: "¿Pasa algo?" le pregunto.
sn.e: "Is something wrong?" I ask him.

sn.s: "Dijiste que ibas a venir ayer y no llegaste."
sn.e: "You said you'd come yesterday and you didn't show up."

sn.s: "Creo que hay un malentendido," digo.
sn.e: "I think there's a misunderstanding," I say.

sn.s: "Yo entendí que era hoy, no ayer."
sn.e: "I understood it was today, not yesterday."

sn.s: "Ah, entonces me equivoqué yo," dice él.
sn.e: "Ah, then I was the one who was wrong," he says.

sn.s: "No, tal vez no me expliqué bien."
sn.e: "No, maybe I didn't explain myself well."

sn.s: "Disculpá la confusión."
sn.e: "Sorry for the confusion."

sn.s: "Tranquilo, fue culpa de los dos," dice riendo.
sn.e: "Relax, it was both our faults," he says, laughing.

sn.s: "Quería aclararlo para que no quedáramos mal."
sn.e: "I wanted to clear it up so we wouldn't be on bad terms."

sn.s: "Todo bien, hermano. Ya quedó arreglado."
sn.e: "All good, brother. It's sorted now."

sn.s: Aclarar un malentendido salva una amistad.
sn.e: Clearing up a misunderstanding saves a friendship.

sn.s: Pedir perdón no es perder; es cuidar el vínculo.
sn.e: Apologizing isn't losing; it's protecting the bond.

sn.s: Hablar las cosas evita que crezcan.
sn.e: Talking things out keeps them from growing.

sn.s: En la cena, hablamos de la educación.
sn.e: At dinner, we talk about education.

sn.s: "¿Qué opinás vos del tema?" me preguntan.
sn.e: "What's your opinion on the topic?" they ask me.

sn.s: Ahora puedo dar una opinión completa.
sn.e: Now I can give a full opinion.

sn.s: "Me parece que la educación es lo más importante."
sn.e: "It seems to me that education is the most important thing."

sn.s: "¿Por qué decís eso?" pregunta la hermana de Roberto.
sn.e: "Why do you say that?" Roberto's sister asks.

sn.s: "Porque sin educación, es difícil cambiar las cosas."
sn.e: "Because without education, it's hard to change things."

sn.s: "Sin embargo, también importa el trabajo," dice ella.
sn.e: "However, work matters too," she says.

sn.s: "Claro, las dos van juntas," respondo.
sn.e: "Of course, the two go together," I respond.

sn.s: "Por ejemplo, un buen trabajo necesita estudio."
sn.e: "For example, a good job needs study."

sn.s: "Tenés un buen punto," admite ella.
sn.e: "You have a good point," she admits.

sn.s: Doy razones, ejemplos, y escucho las suyas.
sn.e: I give reasons, examples, and I listen to theirs.

sn.s: No se trata de ganar, sino de pensar juntos.
sn.e: It's not about winning, but about thinking together.

sn.s: Tener una opinión y explicarla: eso es fluidez.
sn.e: Having an opinion and explaining it: that's fluency.

sn.s: Ya converso como uno más en la mesa.
sn.e: Now I converse like one more person at the table.

sn.s: Tengo una emergencia y necesito ayuda.
sn.e: I have an emergency and need help.

sn.s: Mi computadora se dañó antes de un trabajo importante.
sn.e: My computer broke before an important job.

sn.s: Llamo a Roberto, un poco nervioso.
sn.e: I call Roberto, a little nervous.

sn.s: "Roberto, ¿te puedo pedir un favor grande?"
sn.e: "Roberto, can I ask you a big favor?"

sn.s: "Claro, decime. ¿Qué necesitás?"
sn.e: "Of course, tell me. What do you need?"

sn.s: "¿Me podrías prestar tu computadora unos días?"
sn.e: "Could you lend me your computer for a few days?"

sn.s: "Sé que es mucha molestia," agrego.
sn.e: "I know it's a big imposition," I add.

sn.s: "No es molestia. Para eso están los amigos."
sn.e: "It's no trouble. That's what friends are for."

sn.s: "Te la cuido y te la devuelvo el viernes."
sn.e: "I'll take care of it and return it Friday."

sn.s: "Tranquilo, confío en vos," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Relax, I trust you," Roberto says.

sn.s: "De verdad te lo agradezco mucho."
sn.e: "I really appreciate it a lot."

sn.s: Pedir un favor grande requiere confianza.
sn.e: Asking a big favor requires trust.

sn.s: Y cumplir lo prometido la mantiene.
sn.e: And keeping your promise maintains it.

sn.s: 'Podría' y 'te agradezco' abren muchas puertas.
sn.e: 'Could you' and 'I appreciate it' open many doors.

sn.s: Teníamos planes para ir a la playa el sábado.
sn.e: We had plans to go to the beach on Saturday.

sn.s: Pero el carro de Roberto se dañó.
sn.e: But Roberto's car broke down.

sn.s: "Se canceló el plan," dice, triste.
sn.e: "The plan's off," he says, sad.

sn.s: "Tranquilo, buscamos un plan B," respondo.
sn.e: "Relax, we'll find a plan B," I respond.

sn.s: "¿Qué hacemos entonces?" pregunta.
sn.e: "What do we do then?" he asks.

sn.s: "Podemos tomar el bus. Llegaremos un poco tarde."
sn.e: "We can take the bus. We'll arrive a little late."

sn.s: "Pero igual tendremos toda la tarde," agrego.
sn.e: "But we'll still have the whole afternoon," I add.

sn.s: "Buena idea. No había pensado en eso."
sn.e: "Good idea. I hadn't thought of that."

sn.s: "Mañana arreglás el carro y todo bien."
sn.e: "Tomorrow you fix the car and all's well."

sn.s: "Tenés razón. Improvisar también es divertido."
sn.e: "You're right. Improvising is fun too."

sn.s: Cuando un plan falla, se busca otro.
sn.e: When one plan fails, you find another.

sn.s: Hablar del futuro: iremos, tendremos, llegaremos.
sn.e: Talking about the future: we'll go, we'll have, we'll arrive.

sn.s: La flexibilidad es parte de vivir aquí.
sn.e: Flexibility is part of living here.

sn.s: Al final, lo importante es estar juntos.
sn.e: In the end, what matters is being together.

sn.s: Un conocido me pide dinero prestado otra vez.
sn.e: An acquaintance asks to borrow money again.

sn.s: Es la tercera vez este mes.
sn.e: It's the third time this month.

sn.s: Quiero ayudar, pero también poner un límite.
sn.e: I want to help, but also set a boundary.

sn.s: "Mirá, te aprecio, pero esta vez no puedo."
sn.e: "Look, I appreciate you, but this time I can't."

sn.s: "¿Por qué no?" pregunta él.
sn.e: "Why not?" he asks.

sn.s: "Lamentablemente, ya no me alcanza este mes."
sn.e: "Unfortunately, I don't have enough this month."

sn.s: Lo digo con calma, pero firme.
sn.e: I say it calmly, but firmly.

sn.s: "Espero que comprendás mi situación."
sn.e: "I hope you understand my situation."

sn.s: "Está bien. Gracias por ser honesto," dice él.
sn.e: "It's okay. Thanks for being honest," he says.

sn.s: "Claro. Te ayudo en otra cosa si puedo."
sn.e: "Of course. I'll help with something else if I can."

sn.s: Decir que no también es una forma de respeto.
sn.e: Saying no is also a form of respect.

sn.s: Respeto por uno mismo y por el otro.
sn.e: Respect for yourself and for the other person.

sn.s: Ser honesto y amable a la vez es posible.
sn.e: Being honest and kind at the same time is possible.

sn.s: Poner un límite en español: una victoria personal.
sn.e: Setting a boundary in Spanish: a personal victory.

sn.s: Tengo una entrevista para un buen puesto.
sn.e: I have an interview for a good position.

sn.s: Estoy nervioso, pero preparado.
sn.e: I'm nervous, but prepared.

sn.s: "Cuénteme sobre su experiencia," dice la jefa.
sn.e: "Tell me about your experience," says the boss.

sn.s: "Tengo cinco años trabajando con computadoras."
sn.e: "I have five years working with computers."

sn.s: "¿Cuáles son sus fortalezas?" pregunta.
sn.e: "What are your strengths?" she asks.

sn.s: "Soy organizado y aprendo rápido."
sn.e: "I'm organized and I learn fast."

sn.s: "También hablo inglés y ahora español."
sn.e: "I also speak English and now Spanish."

sn.s: "¿Por qué quiere trabajar en esta empresa?"
sn.e: "Why do you want to work at this company?"

sn.s: "Porque creo que puedo aportar mucho aquí."
sn.e: "Because I believe I can contribute a lot here."

sn.s: "¿Cuándo estaría disponible?"
sn.e: "When would you be available?"

sn.s: "Puedo empezar cuando usted necesite."
sn.e: "I can start whenever you need."

sn.s: "Me gusta su actitud. Lo llamaremos pronto."
sn.e: "I like your attitude. We'll call you soon."

sn.s: Hablar de mí mismo con seguridad: eso es B1.
sn.e: Talking about myself with confidence: that's B1.

sn.s: Una entrevista en español ya no es imposible.
sn.e: A job interview in Spanish is no longer impossible.

sn.s: En una reunión, alguien no está de acuerdo conmigo.
sn.e: In a meeting, someone disagrees with me.

sn.s: "Creo que su idea no va a funcionar," me dice.
sn.e: "I think your idea won't work," he tells me.

sn.s: Antes me quedaba callado. Ahora no.
sn.e: Before I'd stay quiet. Not anymore.

sn.s: "Respeto su opinión, pero no estoy convencido."
sn.e: "I respect your opinion, but I'm not convinced."

sn.s: "Mi propuesta tiene varias ventajas," explico.
sn.e: "My proposal has several advantages," I explain.

sn.s: "Por ejemplo, ahorra tiempo y dinero."
sn.e: "For example, it saves time and money."

sn.s: "Pero es arriesgado," insiste él.
sn.e: "But it's risky," he insists.

sn.s: "Entiendo el riesgo, y aun así lo mantengo."
sn.e: "I understand the risk, and I still stand by it."

sn.s: "Tengo evidencia de que ya funcionó antes."
sn.e: "I have evidence that it worked before."

sn.s: Defiendo mi postura sin faltar al respeto.
sn.e: I defend my position without being disrespectful.

sn.s: "Bueno, escuchemos a los demás," dice la jefa.
sn.e: "Well, let's hear the others," says the boss.

sn.s: No cedí solo por miedo a hablar.
sn.e: I didn't give in just out of fear of speaking.

sn.s: Mantener mi punto, con respeto y razones.
sn.e: Holding my point, with respect and reasons.

sn.s: Esto es tener voz propia en otro idioma.
sn.e: This is having your own voice in another language.

sn.s: En la fiesta de Roberto, conozco a alguien.
sn.e: At Roberto's party, I meet someone.

sn.s: Se llama Lucía. Tiene una sonrisa linda.
sn.e: Her name is Lucía. She has a lovely smile.

sn.s: Platicamos toda la noche.
sn.e: We chat all night.

sn.s: Me pongo un poco nervioso con ella.
sn.e: I get a little nervous around her.

sn.s: "¿De dónde sos?" me pregunta con una mirada dulce.
sn.e: "Where are you from?" she asks with a sweet look.

sn.s: Le cuento de mí, y ella me escucha de verdad.
sn.e: I tell her about myself, and she really listens.

sn.s: Hay algo especial en su forma de ser.
sn.e: There's something special about the way she is.

sn.s: "Me gusta hablar con vos," le digo, tímido.
sn.e: "I like talking with you," I say, shy.

sn.s: "A mí también," responde sonriendo.
sn.e: "Me too," she answers, smiling.

sn.s: Siento algo en el corazón que no esperaba.
sn.e: I feel something in my heart I wasn't expecting.

sn.s: "Ojalá nos veamos otra vez," me atrevo a decir.
sn.e: "I hope we see each other again," I dare to say.

sn.s: "Claro que sí," dice ella.
sn.e: "Of course," she says.

sn.s: 'Ojalá' — esa palabra para los deseos del corazón.
sn.e: 'Ojalá' — that word for the wishes of the heart.

sn.s: Esa noche, algo nuevo empieza.
sn.e: That night, something new begins.

sn.s: Lucía y yo pasamos mucho tiempo juntos.
sn.e: Lucía and I spend a lot of time together.

sn.s: Cada día la quiero más.
sn.e: Every day I care for her more.

sn.s: En español, 'te quiero' es para el cariño.
sn.e: In Spanish, 'te quiero' is for affection.

sn.s: 'Te amo' es más fuerte, más profundo.
sn.e: 'Te amo' is stronger, deeper.

sn.s: Una tarde, le tomo la mano.
sn.e: One afternoon, I take her hand.

sn.s: "Lucía, te quiero mucho," le digo.
sn.e: "Lucía, I care for you a lot," I tell her.

sn.s: Ella me da un abrazo fuerte.
sn.e: She gives me a tight hug.

sn.s: "Yo también te quiero," me responde.
sn.e: "I care for you too," she answers.

sn.s: "Me importás de verdad," agrego.
sn.e: "You really matter to me," I add.

sn.s: Siento que el corazón me late fuerte.
sn.e: I feel my heart beating hard.

sn.s: "¿Sos feliz conmigo?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "Are you happy with me?" she asks.

sn.s: "Muy feliz. Nunca había sentido esto."
sn.e: "Very happy. I've never felt this."

sn.s: Decir 'te quiero' en otro idioma es valiente.
sn.e: Saying 'I care for you' in another language is brave.

sn.s: El amor también se aprende, palabra por palabra.
sn.e: Love is also learned, word by word.

sn.s: Lucía quiere presentarme a su familia.
sn.e: Lucía wants to introduce me to her family.

sn.s: "Espero que les caigas bien," me dice.
sn.e: "I hope they like you," she tells me.

sn.s: Llego con flores para su mamá.
sn.e: I arrive with flowers for her mom.

sn.s: "Mucho gusto, doña. Lucía me habla mucho de usted."
sn.e: "Nice to meet you, ma'am. Lucía talks about you a lot."

sn.s: "Qué detalle tan lindo," dice su mamá.
sn.e: "What a lovely gesture," her mom says.

sn.s: Su papá me da la mano con firmeza.
sn.e: Her dad shakes my hand firmly.

sn.s: "Así que vos sos el que la hace feliz," dice.
sn.e: "So you're the one who makes her happy," he says.

sn.s: "Hago todo lo posible," respondo con respeto.
sn.e: "I do everything I can," I respond respectfully.

sn.s: Comemos juntos y la plática fluye.
sn.e: We eat together and the conversation flows.

sn.s: Quiero causar una buena impresión.
sn.e: I want to make a good impression.

sn.s: "Espero que se sienta como en casa," dice la mamá.
sn.e: "I hope you feel at home," the mom says.

sn.s: "Ya me siento así. Gracias por recibirme."
sn.e: "I already do. Thank you for having me."

sn.s: Al final, Lucía me susurra: "Les encantaste."
sn.e: At the end, Lucía whispers: "They loved you."

sn.s: Ser aceptado por su familia lo es todo.
sn.e: Being accepted by her family means everything.

lessons.title: Una conversación difícil
lessons.desc: Being vulnerable with someone you love

sn.s: Hay algo que me cuesta decirle a Lucía.
sn.e: There's something hard for me to tell Lucía.

sn.s: Tengo miedo de hablar de mis sentimientos.
sn.e: I'm afraid to talk about my feelings.

sn.s: "¿Qué te pasa? Te noto callado," me dice.
sn.e: "What's wrong? You seem quiet," she tells me.

sn.s: Respiro hondo y decido ser sincero.
sn.e: I breathe deep and decide to be honest.

sn.s: "A veces tengo miedo de no ser suficiente."
sn.e: "Sometimes I'm afraid I'm not enough."

sn.s: Es difícil mostrarme vulnerable.
sn.e: It's hard to show myself vulnerable.

sn.s: Lucía me toma la mano y me escucha.
sn.e: Lucía takes my hand and listens.

sn.s: "Gracias por confiar en mí," dice con dulzura.
sn.e: "Thank you for trusting me," she says tenderly.

sn.s: "Para mí, vos sos más que suficiente."
sn.e: "To me, you are more than enough."

sn.s: "Quiero que sepás que siempre te apoyo."
sn.e: "I want you to know I always support you."

sn.s: Sus palabras me quitan un peso enorme.
sn.e: Her words lift an enormous weight off me.

sn.s: "Hablar de esto nos acerca," le digo.
sn.e: "Talking about this brings us closer," I tell her.

sn.s: Abrir el corazón da miedo, pero también libera.
sn.e: Opening your heart is scary, but it also frees you.

sn.s: El amor verdadero se construye con honestidad.
sn.e: True love is built with honesty.

sn.s: Tengo que viajar a mi país por dos semanas.
sn.e: I have to travel to my country for two weeks.

sn.s: Es la primera vez que me separo de Lucía.
sn.e: It's the first time I'm apart from Lucía.

sn.s: Desde el primer día, la extraño mucho.
sn.e: From the first day, I miss her a lot.

sn.s: La llamo por teléfono cada noche.
sn.e: I call her on the phone every night.

sn.s: "Te extraño tanto," le digo.
sn.e: "I miss you so much," I tell her.

sn.s: "Yo también. La casa se siente vacía," responde.
sn.e: "Me too. The house feels empty," she answers.

sn.s: "Ojalá pasen rápido estos días."
sn.e: "I hope these days pass quickly."

sn.s: La distancia me enseña cuánto me importa.
sn.e: The distance teaches me how much she matters.

sn.s: Pienso en su sonrisa, en sus abrazos.
sn.e: I think of her smile, her hugs.

sn.s: "Cuando regrese, te voy a abrazar fuerte."
sn.e: "When I get back, I'm going to hug you tight."

sn.s: "Te espero con todo el corazón," dice ella.
sn.e: "I'll wait for you with all my heart," she says.

sn.s: 'Ojalá' — el deseo de volver pronto a sus brazos.
sn.e: 'Ojalá' — the wish to return soon to her arms.

sn.s: Extrañar a alguien es saber que es importante.
sn.e: Missing someone is knowing they're important.

sn.s: El amor no entiende de distancias.
sn.e: Love doesn't understand distances.

sn.s: La abuela de Lucía está enferma.
sn.e: Lucía's grandmother is sick.

sn.s: Toda la familia se une para cuidarla.
sn.e: The whole family comes together to care for her.

sn.s: "¿Te molesta si ayudo?" le pregunto a Lucía.
sn.e: "Do you mind if I help?" I ask Lucía.

sn.s: "Para nada. Significa mucho para mí," responde.
sn.e: "Not at all. It means a lot to me," she answers.

sn.s: Acompaño a la abuela y le hago compañía.
sn.e: I sit with the grandmother and keep her company.

sn.s: "Sos un buen muchacho," me dice ella, débil.
sn.e: "You're a good young man," she tells me, weak.

sn.s: "Espero que se mejore pronto, doña."
sn.e: "I hope you get better soon, ma'am."

sn.s: Cuidar a alguien requiere paciencia y amor.
sn.e: Caring for someone requires patience and love.

sn.s: Lucía me mira con ojos llenos de cariño.
sn.e: Lucía looks at me with eyes full of affection.

sn.s: "Ver cómo cuidás a mi abuela me enamora más."
sn.e: "Seeing how you care for my grandma makes me love you more."

sn.s: En la familia, los problemas se cargan juntos.
sn.e: In the family, burdens are carried together.

sn.s: "Ojalá tengamos muchos años más con ella."
sn.e: "I hope we have many more years with her."

sn.s: Aquí aprendí que la familia se cuida sin condiciones.
sn.e: Here I learned that family is cared for without conditions.

sn.s: Pertenecer a una familia es también cuidarla.
sn.e: Belonging to a family is also caring for it.

sn.s: Lucía y yo tuvimos nuestra primera pelea.
sn.e: Lucía and I had our first fight.

sn.s: Discutimos por algo pequeño que creció.
sn.e: We argued over something small that grew.

sn.s: Los dos dijimos cosas sin pensar.
sn.e: We both said things without thinking.

sn.s: Después de un rato, me calmo y pienso.
sn.e: After a while, I calm down and think.

sn.s: Voy a buscarla. "Lucía, hablemos, por favor."
sn.e: I go find her. "Lucía, let's talk, please."

sn.s: "Perdoná lo que dije. Estaba molesto."
sn.e: "Forgive what I said. I was upset."

sn.s: "Yo también lo siento," dice ella, suave.
sn.e: "I'm sorry too," she says, softly.

sn.s: "No quiero herirte nunca," le digo.
sn.e: "I never want to hurt you," I tell her.

sn.s: "Quiero que entendás cómo me sentí."
sn.e: "I want you to understand how I felt."

sn.s: Nos escuchamos con calma, sin gritar.
sn.e: We listen to each other calmly, without shouting.

sn.s: "Las parejas también discuten. Lo importante es reconciliarse."
sn.e: "Couples argue too. What matters is making up."

sn.s: Nos abrazamos y el enojo desaparece.
sn.e: We hug and the anger disappears.

sn.s: Pelear bien y perdonar es parte del amor.
sn.e: Fighting fairly and forgiving is part of love.

sn.s: Cada desacuerdo superado nos hace más fuertes.
sn.e: Every disagreement overcome makes us stronger.

sn.s: Es nuestro aniversario de un año juntos.
sn.e: It's our anniversary of one year together.

sn.s: Quiero decirle a Lucía lo que siento de verdad.
sn.e: I want to tell Lucía what I truly feel.

sn.s: "Lucía, quiero que sepás algo importante."
sn.e: "Lucía, I want you to know something important."

sn.s: "Desde que te conocí, mi vida cambió."
sn.e: "Since I met you, my life changed."

sn.s: "Quiero que entendás cuánto te amo."
sn.e: "I want you to understand how much I love you."

sn.s: Esta vez digo 'te amo', no solo 'te quiero'.
sn.e: This time I say 'te amo,' not just 'te quiero.'

sn.s: "Me siento afortunado de tenerte," agrego.
sn.e: "I feel lucky to have you," I add.

sn.s: A Lucía se le llenan los ojos de lágrimas.
sn.e: Lucía's eyes fill with tears.

sn.s: "Yo también te amo, con toda mi alma."
sn.e: "I love you too, with all my soul."

sn.s: "Ojalá pasemos muchos años más juntos."
sn.e: "I hope we spend many more years together."

sn.s: "Te prometo cuidar de lo nuestro," le digo.
sn.e: "I promise to take care of what we have," I tell her.

sn.s: Decir 'te amo' en español ya no me da miedo.
sn.e: Saying 'I love you' in Spanish no longer scares me.

sn.s: El subjuntivo: quiero que sepás, ojalá pasemos.
sn.e: The subjunctive: I want you to know, I hope we spend.

sn.s: Es el idioma del corazón que espera y desea.
sn.e: It's the language of the heart that hopes and wishes.

sn.s: Una noche, Lucía y yo hablamos del futuro.
sn.e: One night, Lucía and I talk about the future.

sn.s: "¿Cómo te imaginás nuestra vida?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "How do you imagine our life?" she asks me.

sn.s: "Sueño con una casa pequeña, con un jardín."
sn.e: "I dream of a small house, with a garden."

sn.s: "Ojalá podamos tenerla algún día," dice ella.
sn.e: "I hope we can have it someday," she says.

sn.s: "Quiero que construyamos algo juntos," le digo.
sn.e: "I want us to build something together," I tell her.

sn.s: "Yo también lo deseo con todo el corazón."
sn.e: "I want that too, with all my heart."

sn.s: Hablamos de viajes, de planes, de esperanzas.
sn.e: We talk about trips, plans, hopes.

sn.s: "Espero que siempre nos apoyemos," dice Lucía.
sn.e: "I hope we always support each other," Lucía says.

sn.s: "Pase lo que pase, vamos a estar juntos."
sn.e: "No matter what happens, we'll be together."

sn.s: El futuro se siente posible a su lado.
sn.e: The future feels possible by her side.

sn.s: "Compartir un sueño es un compromiso," pienso.
sn.e: "Sharing a dream is a commitment," I think.

sn.s: No sé qué traerá la vida, pero la quiero a ella.
sn.e: I don't know what life will bring, but I want her in it.

sn.s: Planear un futuro juntos es un acto de amor.
sn.e: Planning a future together is an act of love.

sn.s: Y ojalá ese futuro apenas comienza.
sn.e: And hopefully that future is just beginning.

sn.s: Ha pasado más de un año desde que llegué.
sn.e: More than a year has passed since I arrived.

sn.s: Una tarde, miro a mi alrededor y reflexiono.
sn.e: One afternoon, I look around and reflect.

sn.s: Tengo a Lucía, su familia, mis amigos.
sn.e: I have Lucía, her family, my friends.

sn.s: Llegué sin saber una palabra de español.
sn.e: I arrived without knowing a word of Spanish.

sn.s: Ahora hablo, río, y amo en este idioma.
sn.e: Now I speak, laugh, and love in this language.

sn.s: "¿En qué pensás?" me pregunta Lucía.
sn.e: "What are you thinking about?" Lucía asks me.

sn.s: "En lo afortunado que soy," le respondo.
sn.e: "About how lucky I am," I answer.

sn.s: "Este lugar se volvió mi hogar."
sn.e: "This place became my home."

sn.s: "Aquí encontré raíces que no esperaba."
