sn.e: "Here I found roots I didn't expect."

sn.s: "Te valoro a vos y a todo lo que tengo."
sn.e: "I value you and everything I have."

sn.s: "Me siento bendecido," digo, agradecido.
sn.e: "I feel blessed," I say, grateful.

sn.s: Lo que importa no son las cosas, sino la gente.
sn.e: What matters isn't things, but people.

sn.s: "Ojalá nunca olvide de dónde vengo," pienso.
sn.e: "I hope I never forget where I come from," I think.

sn.s: Aprender un idioma fue, al final, aprender a pertenecer.
sn.e: Learning a language was, in the end, learning to belong.

sn.s: Roberto me saluda diferente hoy.
sn.e: Roberto greets me differently today.

sn.s: "¡Ey, maje! ¿Qué te contás?"
sn.e: "Hey, dude! What's up with you?"

sn.s: 'Maje' es como 'dude' entre amigos.
sn.e: 'Maje' is like 'dude' between friends.

sn.s: "Aquí nomás, maje. ¿Y vos?" respondo.
sn.e: "Just here, dude. And you?" I respond.

sn.s: "¡Uy, ya hablás como nica!" se ríe.
sn.e: "Whoa, you already talk like a Nica!" he laughs.

sn.s: Usar 'maje' es señal de confianza.
sn.e: Using 'maje' is a sign of trust.

sn.s: Pero ojo: solo con amigos, no con extraños.
sn.e: But careful: only with friends, not with strangers.

sn.s: "Vení, maje, vamos a echar relajo," dice.
sn.e: "Come on, dude, let's go mess around," he says.

sn.s: 'Echar relajo' es pasarla bien, bromear.
sn.e: 'Echar relajo' is to have fun, to joke around.

sn.s: "Dale pues, maje. Pero pagás vos," bromeo.
sn.e: "Okay then, dude. But you pay," I joke.

sn.s: "¡Ideay! Qué tacaño," se ríe.
sn.e: "Come on! What a cheapskate," he laughs.

sn.s: Hablar con confianza me hace sentir parte del grupo.
sn.e: Talking casually makes me feel part of the group.

sn.s: Ya no soy el extranjero formal.
sn.e: I'm no longer the formal foreigner.

sn.s: Ahora soy el maje que habla como ellos.
sn.e: Now I'm the dude who talks like them.

sn.s: Los nicas tienen palabras para todo.
sn.e: Nicas have words for everything.

sn.s: La más famosa es 'ideay'.
sn.e: The most famous is 'ideay'.

sn.s: Sirve para sorpresa, saludo, o reclamo.
sn.e: It works for surprise, greeting, or complaint.

sn.s: "¡Ideay! ¿Dónde andabas?" me dice Lucía.
sn.e: "Hey! Where were you?" Lucía says to me.

sn.s: "Ahí, en el trabajo, pues," respondo.
sn.e: "There, at work, you know," I respond.

sn.s: 'Pues' va al final de casi todo.
sn.e: 'Pues' goes at the end of almost everything.

sn.s: "Fíjate que hoy vi a Roberto," le cuento.
sn.e: "So get this, today I saw Roberto," I tell her.

sn.s: "¿Ah sí? ¡No me digás!" responde ella.
sn.e: "Oh yeah? You don't say!" she responds.

sn.s: "Imaginate que se va a casar."
sn.e: "Imagine, he's getting married."

sn.s: "¡Vaya! ¡Qué barbaridad!" dice sorprendida.
sn.e: "Wow! How incredible!" she says, surprised.

sn.s: Estas palabritas le dan sabor a todo.
sn.e: These little words give flavor to everything.

sn.s: Sin ellas, sonás como un libro.
sn.e: Without them, you sound like a book.

sn.s: Con ellas, sonás como de aquí.
sn.e: With them, you sound like you're from here.

sn.s: Ideay, pues, así se habla en Nicaragua.
sn.e: Well hey, that's how you talk in Nicaragua.

sn.s: El reto más grande es la velocidad.
sn.e: The biggest challenge is the speed.

sn.s: Los nicas hablan rápido y se comen letras.
sn.e: Nicas talk fast and swallow letters.

sn.s: Dicen 'pa' en vez de 'para'.
sn.e: They say 'pa' instead of 'para'.

sn.s: 'Ta bien' en vez de 'está bien'.
sn.e: 'Ta bien' instead of 'está bien'.

sn.s: Al principio me perdía todo el tiempo.
sn.e: At first I got lost all the time.

sn.s: "Más despacio, por favor," pedía yo.
sn.e: "Slower, please," I'd ask.

sn.s: Pero poco a poco, mi oído se acostumbra.
sn.e: But little by little, my ear gets used to it.

sn.s: Ahora capto más, aunque no todo.
sn.e: Now I catch more, though not everything.

sn.s: "¿Vah pal centro?" me pregunta alguien.
sn.e: "You headin' downtown?" someone asks me.

sn.s: Antes no entendía. Ahora sí.
sn.e: Before I didn't understand. Now I do.

sn.s: "Sí, ahí voy," respondo sin pensar.
sn.e: "Yeah, on my way," I respond without thinking.

sn.s: Entender el habla rápida es medio idioma.
sn.e: Understanding fast speech is half the language.

sn.s: Ya no pido que repitan tanto.
sn.e: I don't ask them to repeat as much anymore.

sn.s: El oído entrenado es la clave de la fluidez.
sn.e: A trained ear is the key to fluency.

sn.s: El nica tiene su propio vocabulario.
sn.e: Nica has its own vocabulary.

sn.s: Un 'chunche' es cualquier cosa sin nombre.
sn.e: A 'chunche' is any thingamajig without a name.

sn.s: "Pasame ese chunche," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Pass me that thingy," Roberto says.

sn.s: Un 'chavalo' o una 'chavala' es un niño o un joven.
sn.e: A 'cipote' or 'chavalo' is a kid or young person.

sn.s: Si algo es 'tuani' o 'deacachimba', es genial.
sn.e: If something is 'tuani' or 'deacachimba', it's awesome.

sn.s: "Esa fiesta estuvo deacachimba," digo.
sn.e: "That party was awesome," I say.

sn.s: 'Pinche' significa tacaño o de mala calidad.
sn.e: 'Pinche' means stingy or low quality.

sn.s: A mí me dicen 'chele' por mi piel clara.
sn.e: They call me 'chele' for my light skin.

sn.s: Si tomás mucho, al día siguiente tenés 'goma'.
sn.e: If you drink a lot, the next day you have a hangover.

sn.s: "Ando con una goma terrible," se queja Roberto.
sn.e: "I've got a terrible hangover," Roberto complains.

sn.s: Cada palabra nueva me acerca más a ellos.
sn.e: Each new word brings me closer to them.

sn.s: El slang no se aprende en libros.
sn.e: Slang isn't learned in books.

sn.s: Se aprende en la calle, con la gente.
sn.e: It's learned in the street, with the people.

sn.s: Y entenderlo es entrar en su mundo.
sn.e: And understanding it is entering their world.

sn.s: El humor nica es rápido y pícaro.
sn.e: Nica humor is quick and cheeky.

sn.s: Les encanta 'vacilar', o sea bromear.
sn.e: They love to 'vacilar,' meaning to joke around.

sn.s: Roberto siempre me toma el pelo.
sn.e: Roberto always pulls my leg.

sn.s: "Maje, con ese español ya casi parecés humano," se ríe.
sn.e: "Dude, with that Spanish you almost seem human now," he laughs.

sn.s: Antes me ofendía. Ahora lo entiendo.
sn.e: Before I'd get offended. Now I get it.

sn.s: Si te vacilan, es que te quieren.
sn.e: If they tease you, it means they like you.

sn.s: "Y vos con esa panza ya parecés nica," le devuelvo.
sn.e: "And you with that belly already look like a Nica," I shoot back.

sn.s: Todos sueltan la carcajada.
sn.e: Everyone bursts out laughing.

sn.s: "¡Uy, el chele aprendió a vacilar!" dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Whoa, the foreigner learned to joke!" Roberto says.

sn.s: Devolver una broma es ganarse el respeto.
sn.e: Returning a joke earns you respect.

sn.s: El humor es el último nivel de un idioma.
sn.e: Humor is the final level of a language.

sn.s: Reírte con ellos es ser uno de ellos.
sn.e: Laughing with them is being one of them.

sn.s: Ya no solo entiendo los chistes.
sn.e: I don't just understand the jokes anymore.

sn.s: Ahora los hago yo también.
sn.e: Now I make them too.

sn.s: Los nicas le ponen 'ito' a casi todo.
sn.e: Nicas add 'ito' to almost everything.

sn.s: No es solo tamaño; es cariño y suavidad.
sn.e: It's not just size; it's affection and softness.

sn.s: "¿Querés un cafecito?" pregunta doña Marta.
sn.e: "Want a little coffee?" doña Marta asks.

sn.s: No es un café pequeño. Es un café con cariño.
sn.e: It's not a small coffee. It's coffee with affection.

sn.s: "Sí, gracias. Pero esperá un momentito."
sn.e: "Yes, thanks. But wait a little moment."

sn.s: La palabra más tramposa es 'ahorita'.
sn.e: The trickiest word is 'ahorita'.

sn.s: Puede ser 'ya mismo' o 'en un rato'.
sn.e: It can mean 'right now' or 'in a while'.

sn.s: "Ya voy, ahorita," puede ser en cinco minutos.
sn.e: "I'm coming, ahorita," might mean in five minutes.

sn.s: "O en una hora," me advierte Lucía, riendo.
sn.e: "Or in an hour," Lucía warns me, laughing.

sn.s: "Vivís cerquita, ¿verdad?" me preguntan.
sn.e: "You live real close, right?" they ask me.

sn.s: El diminutivo suaviza, acerca, abraza.
sn.e: The diminutive softens, brings close, embraces.

sn.s: "Tomate tu tiempito," me dicen con cariño.
sn.e: "Take your little time," they tell me fondly.

sn.s: Hablar con diminutivos es hablar con el corazón.
sn.e: Speaking with diminutives is speaking with the heart.

sn.s: Un poquito de 'ito' y ya sonás más dulce.
sn.e: A little bit of 'ito' and you sound sweeter.

sn.s: A veces los nicas no dicen 'no' directamente.
sn.e: Sometimes Nicas don't say 'no' directly.

sn.s: Dicen cosas suaves para no ser groseros.
sn.e: They say soft things to avoid being rude.

sn.s: Invito a un conocido a una fiesta.
sn.e: I invite an acquaintance to a party.

sn.s: "Fijáte que tal vez, ahí veo," me dice.
sn.e: "Well, maybe, I'll see," he tells me.

sn.s: Antes pensaba que era un 'sí'.
sn.e: Before I thought that was a 'yes'.

sn.s: Pero 'ahí veo' muchas veces significa 'no'.
sn.e: But 'I'll see' often means 'no'.

sn.s: Lucía me explica el código.
sn.e: Lucía explains the code to me.

sn.s: "Si dicen 'quizás' o 'tal vez', no esperés mucho."
sn.e: "If they say 'maybe,' don't expect much."

sn.s: "Es una forma amable de decir que no."
sn.e: "It's a polite way of saying no."

sn.s: Aprendo a leer lo que no se dice.
sn.e: I learn to read what isn't said.

sn.s: El tono, la pausa, la mirada: todo habla.
sn.e: The tone, the pause, the look: it all speaks.

sn.s: Entender lo sutil es entender la cultura.
sn.e: Understanding the subtle is understanding the culture.

sn.s: Ya no me tomo todo tan literal.
sn.e: I no longer take everything so literally.

sn.s: Escuchar bien es también leer entre líneas.
sn.e: Listening well is also reading between the lines.

sn.s: Roberto organiza una juntada en su casa.
sn.e: Roberto organizes a get-together at his place.

sn.s: "Vení, maje, va a estar tuani," me dice.
sn.e: "Come, dude, it's gonna be awesome," he tells me.

sn.s: Llego y el ambiente está deacachimba.
sn.e: I arrive and the vibe is awesome.

sn.s: Hay birras, música, y mucho relajo.
sn.e: There are beers, music, and lots of fun.

sn.s: "¡Ideay, chele! Pensé que no venías," grita alguien.
sn.e: "Hey, foreigner! I thought you weren't coming," someone shouts.

sn.s: "¡Aquí ando, pues! No me lo iba a perder."
sn.e: "Here I am! I wasn't gonna miss it."

sn.s: Bailamos, contamos chistes, la pasamos bien.
sn.e: We dance, tell jokes, have a good time.

sn.s: "Este chele ya chivea como nica," se ríen.
sn.e: "This foreigner already parties like a Nica," they laugh.

sn.s: La parranda sigue hasta tarde.
sn.e: The party goes on late.

sn.s: "¿Nos desvelamos hasta el amanecer?" propone Roberto.
sn.e: "Shall we stay up till dawn?" Roberto proposes.

sn.s: "¡Dale pues! Mañana descanso."
sn.e: "Okay then! I'll rest tomorrow."

sn.s: Entre amigos, el tiempo no importa.
sn.e: Among friends, time doesn't matter.

sn.s: Ya no soy invitado: soy parte de la juntada.
sn.e: I'm not a guest anymore: I'm part of the crew.

sn.s: Pertenecer se siente así, en confianza y relajo.
sn.e: Belonging feels like this — in trust and good fun.

sn.s: El humor nica adora el doble sentido.
sn.e: Nica humor loves double meanings.

sn.s: Una frase normal puede tener picardía escondida.
sn.e: A normal phrase can have hidden mischief.

sn.s: Roberto dice algo y todos se ríen.
sn.e: Roberto says something and everyone laughs.

sn.s: Yo no entiendo el chiste al principio.
sn.e: I don't get the joke at first.

sn.s: "Es de doble sentido, maje," me explica Lucía.
sn.e: "It's a double meaning, dude," Lucía explains.

sn.s: "La frase suena inocente, pero tiene malicia."
sn.e: "The phrase sounds innocent, but it's cheeky."

sn.s: Cuando por fin lo pillo, me río fuerte.
sn.e: When I finally catch it, I laugh hard.

sn.s: "¡Ya entendiste! Te estás poniendo malicioso," bromea ella.
sn.e: "You got it! You're getting mischievous," she teases.

sn.s: Es un humor pícaro, pero casi siempre sano.
sn.e: It's a cheeky humor, but almost always good-natured.

sn.s: Requiere ingenio y un oído fino.
sn.e: It requires wit and a sharp ear.

sn.s: Pillar un doble sentido es un logro grande.
sn.e: Catching a double meaning is a big achievement.

sn.s: Significa que pensás en español, no que traducís.
sn.e: It means you think in Spanish, not that you translate.

sn.s: Me sonrojo un poco, pero me río con ellos.
sn.e: I blush a little, but I laugh with them.

sn.s: El día que captás el doble sentido, ya llegaste.
sn.e: The day you catch the double meaning, you've arrived.

sn.s: Estoy en la pulpería comprando, como siempre.
sn.e: I'm at the corner store shopping, as always.

sn.s: Platico con doña Marta, suelto, natural.
sn.e: I chat with doña Marta, loose, natural.

sn.s: Uso 'maje', 'ideay', 'tuani', sin pensar.
sn.e: I use 'maje', 'ideay', 'tuani', without thinking.

sn.s: Una clienta nueva me escucha hablar.
sn.e: A new customer listens to me talk.

sn.s: "¿De qué parte sos?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "What part are you from?" she asks.

sn.s: "Soy de Estados Unidos," respondo.
sn.e: "I'm from the United States," I respond.

sn.s: "¡No puede ser! Hablás como pinolero," dice.
sn.e: "No way! You talk like a Nicaraguan," she says.

sn.s: 'Pinolero' es como los nicas se dicen a sí mismos.
sn.e: 'Pinolero' is what Nicas call themselves.

sn.s: Es el halago más grande que podía recibir.
sn.e: It's the biggest compliment I could receive.

sn.s: Doña Marta sonríe, orgullosa.
sn.e: Doña Marta smiles, proud.

sn.s: "Es que ya es de aquí," dice ella.
sn.e: "It's because he's from here now," she says.

sn.s: Pienso en el largo camino desde aquel primer 'buenas'.
sn.e: I think of the long road since that first 'buenas'.

sn.s: Llegué sin nada y encontré una voz, una casa, una vida.
sn.e: I arrived with nothing and found a voice, a home, a life.

sn.s: Ya no hablo español: vivo en español.
sn.e: I don't speak Spanish anymore: I live in Spanish.

sn.s: Roberto me enseña el secreto del acento nica.
sn.e: Roberto teaches me the secret of the Nica accent.

sn.s: "Aquí no decimos las eses al final," me explica.
sn.e: "Here we don't say the s's at the end," he explains.

sn.s: En vez de 'los frijoles', decimos 'lo' frijole'.
sn.e: Instead of 'los frijoles', we say 'lo' frijole'.

sn.s: La 's' se aspira o desaparece: 'ehtá' por 'está'.
sn.e: The 's' is aspirated or disappears: 'ehtá' for 'está'.

sn.s: "¿Cómo ehtáh?" suena, no '¿cómo estás?'
sn.e: "¿Cómo ehtáh?" is how it sounds, not '¿cómo estás?'

sn.s: Un mexicano pronuncia cada 's' con cuidado.
sn.e: A Mexican pronounces every 's' carefully.

sn.s: Un español la marca aún más fuerte.
sn.e: A Spaniard marks it even more strongly.

sn.s: Pero el nica la suaviza, la deja ir.
sn.e: But the Nica softens it, lets it go.

sn.s: "Decí 'má o meno' en vez de 'más o menos'," me dice.
sn.e: "Say 'má o meno' instead of 'más o menos'," he tells me.

sn.s: Practico: 'do' cervesa, por favo'.
sn.e: I practice: 'two beers, please' (with dropped s's).

sn.s: "¡Eso! Ya te sale el acento de la costa," se ríe.
sn.e: "That's it! The coastal accent is coming out now," he laughs.

sn.s: Este sonido relajado es puro Nicaragua.
sn.e: This relaxed sound is pure Nicaragua.

sn.s: No es hablar mal: es hablar como de aquí.
sn.e: It's not speaking badly: it's speaking like a local.

sn.s: El oído ya distingue lo nica de lo demás.
sn.e: My ear now distinguishes Nica from the rest.

lessons.title: Voseo a fondo
lessons.desc: Deep voseo: how Nicas really conjugate

sn.s: En Nicaragua nadie usa 'tú'. Todo es 'vos'.
sn.e: In Nicaragua nobody uses 'tú'. Everything is 'vos'.

sn.s: Pero el voseo cambia los verbos, no solo el pronombre.
sn.e: But voseo changes the verbs, not just the pronoun.

sn.s: No es 'tú tienes', sino 'vos tenés'.
sn.e: It's not 'tú tienes', but 'vos tenés'.

sn.s: No es 'ven', sino 'vení'. No es 'mira', sino 'mirá'.
sn.e: It's not 'ven', but 'vení'. Not 'mira', but 'mirá'.

sn.s: Los mandatos llevan el acento al final.
sn.e: Commands carry the accent at the end.

sn.s: "Andá al mercado y traé pan," me pide Lucía.
sn.e: "Go to the market and bring bread," Lucía asks me.

sn.s: "Acordate de la leche también," agrega.
sn.e: "Remember the milk too," she adds.

sn.s: 'Acordate', 'fijate', 'tomate un café': puro voseo.
sn.e: 'Acordate', 'fijate', 'have a coffee': pure voseo.

sn.s: "¿Vos sabés dónde queda?" me pregunta.
sn.e: "Do you know where it is?" she asks me.

sn.s: "Sí, ya sé. Decime si necesitás algo más."
sn.e: "Yes, I know. Tell me if you need anything else."

sn.s: El voseo nica es distinto al de Argentina también.
sn.e: Nica voseo is different from Argentina's too.

sn.s: Cada país que vosea tiene su propio ritmo.
sn.e: Each country that uses voseo has its own rhythm.

sn.s: Dominar el voseo nica es clave para sonar de aquí.
sn.e: Mastering Nica voseo is key to sounding local.

sn.s: Ya no se me escapa ni un 'tú' por error.
sn.e: Not a single 'tú' slips out by mistake anymore.

lessons.title: Palabras solo de aquí
lessons.desc: Words you'll only hear in Nicaragua

sn.s: Hay palabras que solo existen en Nicaragua.
sn.e: There are words that only exist in Nicaragua.

sn.s: Si algo está 'tuani', está buenísimo.
sn.e: If something is 'tuani', it's great.

sn.s: Si está 'deacachimba', está todavía mejor.
sn.e: If it's 'deacachimba', it's even better.

sn.s: Un 'chavalo' es un muchacho joven, y 'maje' es cómo le hablás.
sn.e: A 'chavalo' or 'cipote' is a young kid.

sn.s: Tus 'chereques' son tus cosas, tus chunches.
sn.e: Your 'chereques' are your things, your stuff.

sn.s: "Agarrá tus chereques que ya nos vamos," dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Grab your stuff, we're leaving," Roberto says.

sn.s: Una 'pinta' es la apariencia de alguien.
sn.e: A 'pinta' is someone's appearance.

sn.s: "¡Qué buena pinta tenés hoy!" me dicen.
sn.e: "You look sharp today!" they tell me.

sn.s: Cuando alguien se 'enturca', se enoja.
sn.e: When someone 'se enturca', they get angry.

sn.s: Una 'chochada' es una cosa sin importancia.
sn.e: A 'chochada' is something unimportant.

sn.s: Un mexicano no entendería ninguna de estas.
sn.e: A Mexican wouldn't understand any of these.

sn.s: Son el sabor único del español nicaragüense.
sn.e: They're the unique flavor of Nicaraguan Spanish.

sn.s: Usarlas bien me marca como uno más del barrio.
sn.e: Using them well marks me as one of the neighborhood.

sn.s: Cada palabra nica que aprendo es una insignia.
sn.e: Each Nica word I learn is a badge.

sn.s: No solo cambian las palabras, sino cómo se dicen.
sn.e: It's not just the words, but how they're said.

sn.s: Un mexicano va a 'la tienda'; el nica, a 'la pulpería'.
sn.e: A Mexican goes to 'la tienda'; the Nica, to 'la pulpería'.

sn.s: En otros países 'ocupar' es usar un espacio.
sn.e: In other countries 'ocupar' means to use a space.

sn.s: Aquí 'ocupo' significa 'necesito'.
sn.e: Here 'ocupo' means 'I need'.

sn.s: "Ocupo ir al banco," dice un nica con naturalidad.
sn.e: "I need to go to the bank," a Nica says naturally.

sn.s: Cuando un nica dice 'regaláme', no pide un regalo.
sn.e: When a Nica says 'regaláme', they're not asking for a gift.

sn.s: "Regaláme un vaso de agua" es solo 'dame, por favor'.
sn.e: "Regaláme a glass of water" just means 'please give me'.

sn.s: 'Hacer un mandado' es ir a hacer una diligencia.
sn.e: 'Hacer un mandado' is to run an errand.

sn.s: "Andá hacé un mandadito," me pide doña Marta.
sn.e: "Go run a little errand," doña Marta asks me.

sn.s: Estas formas no se aprenden en una clase normal.
sn.e: These forms aren't learned in a normal class.

sn.s: Se aprenden viviendo entre nicaragüenses.
sn.e: They're learned living among Nicaraguans.

sn.s: Saber qué dice un nica, y cómo, es sonar local.
sn.e: Knowing what a Nica says, and how, is sounding local.

sn.s: Ya pienso en nica, no solo en español.
sn.e: I now think in Nica, not just in Spanish.

sn.s: Y esa diferencia es la que importa aquí.
sn.e: And that difference is the one that matters here.

sn.s: El día de un nica está lleno de sus propias frases.
sn.e: A Nica's day is full of their own phrases.

sn.s: 'Ideay' abre cualquier conversación.
sn.e: 'Ideay' opens any conversation.

sn.s: 'Pues' la cierra: 'ahí nos vemos, pues'.
sn.e: 'Pues' closes it: 'see you, then'.

sn.s: Para decir que sí con ganas: '¡ahuevo!'
sn.e: To say yes with enthusiasm: '¡ahuevo!'

sn.s: 'Dale pues' es el sí más nica de todos.
sn.e: 'Dale pues' is the most Nica yes of all.

sn.s: Cuando algo te gusta mucho, te 'amañás'.
sn.e: When you really like a place, you 'get comfortable' there.

sn.s: "Ya me amañé en este barrio," le digo a Lucía.
sn.e: "I've settled into this neighborhood," I tell Lucía.

sn.s: 'Chinear' es cargar o consentir con cariño a alguien.
sn.e: 'Chinear' is to carry or lovingly pamper someone.

sn.s: "A esa bebé la chinean todos," dice la abuela.
sn.e: "Everyone dotes on that baby," the grandma says.

sn.s: Estas palabras no son de España ni de México.
sn.e: These words aren't from Spain or Mexico.

sn.s: Son el corazón del habla nicaragüense diaria.
sn.e: They're the heart of everyday Nicaraguan speech.

sn.s: Usarlas sin pensar es la prueba de que ya soy de aquí.
sn.e: Using them without thinking proves I'm from here now.

sn.s: "Hablás más nica que muchos nicas," bromea Roberto.
sn.e: "You talk more Nica than many Nicas," Roberto jokes.

sn.s: Y para mí, eso vale más que cualquier diploma.
sn.e: And to me, that's worth more than any diploma.

sn.s: Los nicaragüenses se llaman a sí mismos 'pinoleros'.
sn.e: Nicaraguans call themselves 'pinoleros'.

sn.s: Viene del 'pinol', una bebida de maíz ancestral.
sn.e: It comes from 'pinol', an ancestral corn drink.

sn.s: El maíz está en el alma y en el idioma.
sn.e: Corn is in the soul and in the language.

sn.s: "Somos hijos del maíz," dice el abuelo con orgullo.
sn.e: "We are children of corn," the grandfather says proudly.

sn.s: Hablar de comida es hablar de identidad.
sn.e: Talking about food is talking about identity.

sn.s: El 'gallopinto' no es solo arroz con frijoles.
sn.e: 'Gallopinto' isn't just rice with beans.

sn.s: Es el desayuno que une a todo un país.
sn.e: It's the breakfast that unites a whole country.

sn.s: El 'nacatamal' del domingo es casi una ceremonia.
sn.e: Sunday's 'nacatamal' is almost a ceremony.

sn.s: Cuando uso estas palabras, toco la raíz del país.
sn.e: When I use these words, I touch the country's roots.

sn.s: "Vos ya sabés lo que es ser pinolero," me dice Lucía.
sn.e: "You already know what it is to be pinolero," Lucía tells me.

sn.s: No es solo el idioma; es la tierra, la comida, el orgullo.
sn.e: It's not just the language; it's the land, the food, the pride.

sn.s: Hablar como nica es entender de dónde viene cada palabra.
sn.e: Speaking like a Nica is understanding where each word comes from.

sn.s: Y cada palabra aquí sabe a maíz y a hogar.
sn.e: And every word here tastes of corn and home.

sn.s: Me siento parte de esa herencia ahora.
sn.e: I feel part of that heritage now.

sn.s: Lucía y yo visitamos a su familia en el campo.
sn.e: Lucía and I visit her family in the countryside.

sn.s: El habla del campo es distinta a la de la ciudad.
sn.e: Rural speech is different from the city's.

sn.s: Es más pausada, más dulce, llena de 'usted'.
sn.e: It's slower, sweeter, full of 'usted'.

sn.s: En el campo, el respeto se nota en cada palabra.
sn.e: In the countryside, respect shows in every word.

sn.s: "Pase adelante, mi hijo. Está en su casa," dice don Chico.
sn.e: "Come in, son. Make yourself at home," don Chico says.

sn.s: Aunque acabo de llegar, ya me tratan como familia.
sn.e: Even though I just arrived, they treat me like family.

sn.s: "Aquí madrugamos con los gallos," me cuenta.
sn.e: "Here we rise early with the roosters," he tells me.

sn.s: Habla de la cosecha, de los bueyes, de la tierra.
sn.e: He talks about the harvest, the oxen, the land.

sn.s: Su español es sencillo pero sabio, sin prisa.
sn.e: His Spanish is simple but wise, unhurried.

sn.s: "La tierra no miente, mi hijo," dice despacio.
sn.e: "The land doesn't lie, son," he says slowly.

sn.s: La hospitalidad del campo no tiene igual.
sn.e: Rural hospitality is unmatched.

sn.s: Entender este español es entender el alma rural del país.
sn.e: Understanding this Spanish is understanding the country's rural soul.

sn.s: Me despido con un 'que le vaya bien, don Chico'.
sn.e: I say goodbye with a 'take care, don Chico'.

sn.s: Y él responde: 'vuelva pronto, ya es de la familia'.
sn.e: And he answers: 'come back soon, you're family now'.

sn.s: Roberto y yo jugamos a comparar el español de cada país.
sn.e: Roberto and I play at comparing each country's Spanish.

sn.s: Lo que en México es 'camión', aquí es 'bus'.
sn.e: What in Mexico is 'camión', here is 'bus'.

sn.s: El 'autobús' de España aquí nadie lo dice así.
sn.e: Nobody here says Spain's 'autobús'.

sn.s: Un niño es 'chavalo' aquí, 'chamaco' en México, 'crío' en España.
sn.e: A kid is 'chavalo' here, 'chamaco' in Mexico, 'crío' in Spain.

sn.s: El licor fuerte aquí es 'guaro', no 'trago' ni 'chupito'.
sn.e: Strong liquor here is 'guaro', not 'trago' or 'chupito'.

sn.s: Las sandalias son 'chinelas', no 'chanclas'.
sn.e: Sandals are 'chinelas', not 'chanclas'.

sn.s: Para escribir, el nica pide un 'lapicero', no una 'pluma'.
sn.e: To write, a Nica asks for a 'lapicero', not a 'pluma'.

sn.s: "Cada país tiene su propio diccionario," digo.
sn.e: "Each country has its own dictionary," I say.

sn.s: "Y vos ya tenés el nuestro en la cabeza," responde Roberto.
sn.e: "And you've already got ours in your head," Roberto responds.

sn.s: Saber estas diferencias evita confusiones graciosas.
sn.e: Knowing these differences avoids funny confusions.

sn.s: Pero más que eso, me hace sonar de un lugar: de aquí.
sn.e: But more than that, it makes me sound from one place: here.

sn.s: No hablo 'español neutro'; hablo nicaragüense.
sn.e: I don't speak 'neutral Spanish'; I speak Nicaraguan.

sn.s: Y eso, en cualquier parte, dice de dónde es mi corazón.
sn.e: And that, anywhere, says where my heart is from.

sn.s: El acento es como una bandera que uno lleva al hablar.
sn.e: An accent is like a flag you carry when you speak.

sn.s: Los modismos nicas tienen su propia lógica.
sn.e: Nica idioms have their own logic.

sn.s: 'Andar de goma' es estar crudo después de tomar.
sn.e: 'Andar de goma' is being hungover after drinking.

sn.s: "Hoy ando de goma," se queja Roberto un domingo.
sn.e: "Today I'm hungover," Roberto complains one Sunday.

sn.s: Si algo está 'jodido', está difícil o arruinado.
sn.e: If something's 'jodido', it's hard or ruined.

sn.s: 'Echarse un pega' es tomar una siesta corta.
sn.e: 'Echarse un pega' is to take a short nap.

sn.s: Un 'tranque' es un bloqueo o un atasco en la calle.
sn.e: A 'tranque' is a roadblock or traffic jam.

sn.s: "Había un tranque tremendo," digo, llegando tarde.
sn.e: "There was a huge jam," I say, arriving late.

sn.s: '¡Chocho!' es una exclamación de sorpresa muy nica.
sn.e: '¡Chocho!' is a very Nica exclamation of surprise.

sn.s: 'Zafarse' de algo es librarse o escaparse de eso.
sn.e: 'Zafarse' from something is to get out of it.

sn.s: Estos dichos no se traducen; se sienten.
sn.e: These sayings aren't translated; they're felt.

sn.s: Usar un modismo en el momento justo da mucha risa.
sn.e: Using an idiom at the right moment gets big laughs.

sn.s: "¡Chocho, este chele habla puro nica!" gritan.
sn.e: "Wow, this foreigner speaks pure Nica!" they shout.

sn.s: Los modismos son el último candado del idioma.
sn.e: Idioms are the language's final lock.

sn.s: Y siento que ya tengo casi todas las llaves.
sn.e: And I feel I now have almost all the keys.

sn.s: Viajo a otro país y conozco a unos latinos.
sn.e: I travel to another country and meet some Latinos.

sn.s: Apenas abro la boca, uno me pregunta algo.
sn.e: As soon as I open my mouth, one asks me something.

sn.s: "Vos sos de Nicaragua, ¿verdad?"
sn.e: "You're from Nicaragua, right?"

sn.s: No me pregunta si soy latino. Sabe el país exacto.
sn.e: He doesn't ask if I'm Latino. He knows the exact country.

sn.s: "¿Cómo supiste?" le pregunto, sorprendido.
sn.e: "How did you know?" I ask, surprised.

sn.s: "Por el acento, el voseo, las palabras. Puro nica."
sn.e: "By the accent, the voseo, the words. Pure Nica."

sn.s: Me come las eses, digo 'tuani', voseo sin pensar.
sn.e: I drop my s's, say 'tuani', use voseo without thinking.

sn.s: Mi español tiene una bandera, y es azul y blanco.
sn.e: My Spanish has a flag, and it's blue and white.

sn.s: No hablo un español de ninguna parte.
sn.e: I don't speak a Spanish from nowhere.

sn.s: Hablo el español de un lugar que amo.
sn.e: I speak the Spanish of a place I love.

sn.s: Sonar nica no fue meta de gramática, sino de corazón.
sn.e: Sounding Nica wasn't a grammar goal, but a heart one.

sn.s: Adopté no solo el idioma, sino su acento, su alma.
sn.e: I adopted not just the language, but its accent, its soul.

sn.s: "Pues sí," respondo con orgullo. "Soy de allá."
sn.e: "Well, yes," I answer proudly. "I'm from there."

sn.s: Y al decirlo, siento que es completamente verdad.
sn.e: And saying it, I feel it's completely true.

sn.s: En una reunión seria, noto cómo hablan los profesionales.
sn.e: In a serious meeting, I notice how professionals speak.

sn.s: No usan 'pero'; usan 'no obstante'.
sn.e: They don't use 'pero'; they use 'no obstante' (nonetheless).

sn.s: No dicen 'por eso'; dicen 'por ende' o 'por consiguiente'.
sn.e: They don't say 'por eso'; they say 'por ende' or 'por consiguiente' (therefore).

sn.s: "El plan es bueno; no obstante, tiene riesgos," digo.
sn.e: "The plan is good; nonetheless, it has risks," I say.

sn.s: "Dado que el tiempo apremia, debemos decidir hoy."
sn.e: "Given that time is pressing, we must decide today."

sn.s: 'Asimismo' enlaza ideas con elegancia: 'y también'.
sn.e: 'Asimismo' (likewise) links ideas elegantly: 'and also'.

sn.s: "En cuanto a los costos, los analizaremos después."
sn.e: "As for the costs, we'll analyze them later."

sn.s: 'Pese a' suena más culto que 'a pesar de'.
sn.e: 'Pese a' (despite) sounds more cultured than 'a pesar de'.

sn.s: "Pese a las dudas, en efecto, el proyecto avanza."
sn.e: "Despite the doubts, indeed, the project moves forward."

sn.s: Estos conectores son el andamiaje del habla culta.
sn.e: These connectors are the scaffolding of cultured speech.

sn.s: Un nativo los usa sin pensar; yo aprendí a hacerlo.
sn.e: A native uses them without thinking; I learned to do it.

sn.s: "De ahí que su español suene tan pulido," dice la jefa.
sn.e: "Hence your Spanish sounds so polished," the boss says.

sn.s: Cambiar 'pero' por 'no obstante' eleva todo el discurso.
sn.e: Swapping 'pero' for 'no obstante' elevates the whole speech.

sn.s: Ya no hablo solo correcto: hablo con altura.
sn.e: I no longer speak just correctly: I speak with elevation.

sn.s: Lucía lee mucho, y de ella aprendo adjetivos finos.
sn.e: Lucía reads a lot, and from her I learn refined adjectives.

sn.s: En vez de 'buena idea', dice 'una idea atinada'.
sn.e: Instead of 'good idea', she says 'an apt idea' (atinada).

sn.s: 'Atinado' es acertado, justo, bien pensado.
sn.e: 'Atinado' means apt, accurate, well thought out.

sn.s: Si alguien es muy feliz, está 'dichoso'.
sn.e: If someone is very happy, they're 'dichoso' (blessed/joyful).

sn.s: Un análisis rápido y superficial es 'somero'.
sn.e: A quick, surface-level analysis is 'somero' (cursory).

sn.s: Un fanático intenso es un seguidor 'acérrimo'.
sn.e: An intense fan is an 'acérrimo' (staunch) follower.

sn.s: "Sos muy minucioso con los detalles," me dice Lucía.
sn.e: "You're very meticulous with details," Lucía tells me.

sn.s: Una respuesta firme y sin matices es 'tajante'.
sn.e: A firm, blunt answer is 'tajante' (categorical).

sn.s: Alguien observador y astuto es 'perspicaz'.
sn.e: Someone observant and sharp is 'perspicaz' (perceptive).

sn.s: Una charla agradable y entretenida es 'amena'.
sn.e: A pleasant, entertaining chat is 'amena' (enjoyable).

sn.s: 'La índole' de algo es su naturaleza o carácter.
sn.e: The 'índole' of something is its nature or character.

sn.s: "Es un problema de otra índole," digo con soltura.
sn.e: "It's a problem of another nature," I say smoothly.

sn.s: Estos adjetivos no salen en los libros básicos.
sn.e: These adjectives don't appear in basic books.

sn.s: Pero un nativo culto los tiene siempre a la mano.
sn.e: But a cultured native always has them at hand.

sn.s: En el periódico encuentro verbos que rara vez se hablan.
sn.e: In the newspaper I find verbs rarely spoken aloud.

sn.s: En vez de 'usar un argumento', se 'esgrime' un argumento.
sn.e: Instead of 'use an argument', one 'wields' (esgrime) an argument.

sn.s: 'Ponderar' es considerar algo con cuidado, sopesarlo.
sn.e: 'Ponderar' is to weigh something carefully.

sn.s: "Hay que ponderar bien los riesgos," digo en la reunión.
sn.e: "We must weigh the risks well," I say in the meeting.

sn.s: 'Vislumbrar' es percibir algo de forma tenue o lejana.
sn.e: 'Vislumbrar' is to glimpse something faintly or distantly.

sn.s: "Vislumbro una solución," suena mejor que 'veo una'.
sn.e: "I glimpse a solution" sounds better than 'I see one'.

sn.s: Un tema que provoca debate 'suscita' polémica.
sn.e: A topic that provokes debate 'suscita' (stirs up) controversy.

sn.s: 'Acaecer' es una forma culta de decir 'suceder'.
sn.e: 'Acaecer' is a refined way to say 'to happen'.

sn.s: 'Ahondar' es profundizar: 'ahondemos en el tema'.
sn.e: 'Ahondar' is to delve deeper: 'let's delve into the topic'.

sn.s: 'Recalcar' es enfatizar: 'quiero recalcar un punto'.
sn.e: 'Recalcar' is to stress: 'I want to stress a point'.

sn.s: 'Albergar' una esperanza es guardarla dentro.
sn.e: To 'albergar' (harbor) a hope is to hold it within.

sn.s: "Albergo la esperanza de quedarme aquí," le digo a Lucía.
sn.e: "I harbor the hope of staying here," I tell Lucía.

sn.s: Estos verbos dan precisión y elegancia al hablar.
sn.e: These verbs give precision and elegance to speech.

sn.s: Un nativo los reconoce al instante, aunque no los use a diario.
sn.e: A native recognizes them instantly, even if not used daily.

lessons.title: Palabras que impresionan
lessons.desc: Words that mark a refined speaker

sn.s: Hay palabras que, bien usadas, revelan un dominio profundo.
sn.e: There are words that, used well, reveal deep command.

sn.s: Algo propio de la esencia de una cosa es 'inherente'.
sn.e: Something belonging to a thing's essence is 'inherent'.

sn.s: "El riesgo es inherente a todo cambio," digo.
sn.e: "Risk is inherent to all change," I say.

sn.s: Un resumen breve y claro es 'sucinto'.
sn.e: A brief, clear summary is 'succinct'.

sn.s: "Seré sucinto," anuncio antes de hablar poco y bien.
sn.e: "I'll be succinct," I announce before speaking briefly and well.

sn.s: Algo necesario que no se puede evitar es 'ineludible'.
sn.e: Something necessary that can't be avoided is 'unavoidable'.

sn.s: Algo digno de elogio es 'loable'.
sn.e: Something praiseworthy is 'loable' (laudable).

sn.s: "Tu esfuerzo es loable," me dice la profesora.
sn.e: "Your effort is laudable," the professor tells me.

sn.s: Algo apropiado al tema es 'pertinente'.
sn.e: Something relevant to the topic is 'pertinent'.

sn.s: 'Soslayar' es evitar o esquivar un asunto.
sn.e: 'Soslayar' is to sidestep or dodge a matter.

sn.s: "No quiero soslayar el problema," aclaro.
sn.e: "I don't want to sidestep the problem," I clarify.

sn.s: Lo absolutamente necesario es 'imprescindible'.
sn.e: What's absolutely necessary is 'imprescindible' (indispensable).

sn.s: Estas palabras son el sello de quien domina el idioma.
sn.e: These words are the hallmark of one who masters the language.

sn.s: Y ahora forman parte de mi vocabulario natural.
sn.e: And now they're part of my natural vocabulary.

lessons.title: El registro formal
lessons.desc: Elevated phrasing for writing and speeches

sn.s: Tengo que escribir un correo formal importante.
sn.e: I have to write an important formal email.

sn.s: El registro escrito culto es otro mundo.
sn.e: The cultured written register is another world.

sn.s: No empiezo con 'hola', sino con 'Estimado señor'.
sn.e: I don't start with 'hi', but with 'Dear sir'.

sn.s: "Le escribo para agradecer su pronta respuesta."
sn.e: "I write to thank you for your prompt response."

sn.s: 'Quedo a su disposición' ofrece ayuda con elegancia.
sn.e: 'I remain at your disposal' offers help elegantly.

sn.s: "Conforme a lo acordado, le remito el documento."
sn.e: "In accordance with what we agreed, I send you the document."

sn.s: 'Acatar' es cumplir o seguir una norma.
sn.e: 'Acatar' is to comply with or follow a rule.

sn.s: Quiero 'destacar' lo importante: enfatizarlo con cuidado.
sn.e: I want to 'highlight' the important part: emphasize it carefully.

sn.s: Cierro con 'atentamente', nunca con 'chao'.
sn.e: I close with 'sincerely', never with 'bye'.

sn.s: Cada frase formal tiene su fórmula precisa.
sn.e: Each formal phrase has its precise formula.

sn.s: Saber este registro abre puertas profesionales.
sn.e: Knowing this register opens professional doors.

sn.s: Es la diferencia entre escribir bien y escribir con autoridad.
sn.e: It's the difference between writing well and writing with authority.

sn.s: La respuesta llega: 'Su carta es de lo más cordial y atinada'.
sn.e: The reply comes: 'Your letter is most cordial and apt'.

sn.s: Dominar lo formal y lo coloquial: eso es ser completo.
sn.e: Mastering the formal and the colloquial: that's being complete.

sn.s: Lucía me enseña distinciones que solo un nativo siente.
sn.e: Lucía teaches me distinctions only a native feels.

sn.s: 'Oír' es percibir sonido; 'escuchar' es prestar atención.
sn.e: 'Oír' is to perceive sound; 'escuchar' is to pay attention.

sn.s: "Te oigo, pero no te estaba escuchando," puede pasar.
sn.e: "I hear you, but I wasn't listening," can happen.

sn.s: 'Recordar' es traer a la memoria; 'acordarse' es más íntimo.
sn.e: 'Recordar' is to recall; 'acordarse' is more intimate.

sn.s: Hay diferencia entre 'un viejo amigo' y 'un amigo viejo'.
sn.e: There's a difference between 'an old friend' and 'an elderly friend'.

sn.s: El orden de la palabra cambia el sentido por completo.
sn.e: Word order changes the meaning completely.

sn.s: 'Cierto hombre' y 'un hombre cierto' no son lo mismo.
sn.e: 'A certain man' and 'a sure man' aren't the same.

sn.s: 'Pobre hombre' da lástima; 'hombre pobre' no tiene dinero.
sn.e: 'Pobre hombre' is pitiful; 'hombre pobre' has no money.

sn.s: Apreciar estos matices es percibir el alma del idioma.
sn.e: Appreciating these nuances is perceiving the language's soul.

sn.s: "Ya diferenciás cosas que muchos ni notan," dice Lucía.
sn.e: "You already distinguish things many don't even notice," Lucía says.

sn.s: Un matiz leve puede cambiarlo todo en una frase.
sn.e: A slight nuance can change everything in a sentence.

sn.s: Escoger la palabra exacta es un placer en sí mismo.
sn.e: Choosing the exact word is a pleasure in itself.

sn.s: Estas sutilezas son el territorio del verdadero dominio.
sn.e: These subtleties are the territory of true mastery.

sn.s: Y por fin las habito con naturalidad.
sn.e: And at last I inhabit them naturally.

lessons.title: Sustantivos cultos
lessons.desc: Refined nouns a native grew up with

sn.s: Hay sustantivos que dan peso y belleza a una frase.
sn.e: There are nouns that lend weight and beauty to a phrase.

sn.s: El 'sosiego' es la calma profunda, la paz interior.
sn.e: 'Sosiego' is deep calm, inner peace.

sn.s: "Busco un poco de sosiego," digo tras un día largo.
sn.e: "I seek a bit of tranquility," I say after a long day.

sn.s: Un 'anhelo' es un deseo profundo del corazón.
sn.e: An 'anhelo' is a deep longing of the heart.

sn.s: El 'recelo' es la desconfianza o sospecha.
sn.e: 'Recelo' is distrust or suspicion.

sn.s: Un 'atisbo' es un indicio leve, un primer asomo.
sn.e: An 'atisbo' is a faint hint, a first glimpse.

sn.s: 'Es menester' es una forma culta de 'es necesario'.
sn.e: 'Es menester' is a refined way of 'it's necessary'.

sn.s: 'Hacer hincapié' es insistir o enfatizar algo.
sn.e: 'Hacer hincapié' is to insist on or emphasize something.

sn.s: "Hago hincapié en la importancia de esto," recalco.
sn.e: "I stress the importance of this," I emphasize.

sn.s: El 'auge' es el momento de mayor esplendor.
sn.e: 'Auge' is the moment of greatest splendor (peak).

sn.s: La 'merma' es la disminución o pérdida de algo.
sn.e: 'Merma' is the decrease or loss of something.

sn.s: El 'libre albedrío' es la libertad de elegir.
sn.e: 'Libre albedrío' is free will.

sn.s: Estas palabras vienen de leer, de escuchar, de vivir.
sn.e: These words come from reading, listening, living.

sn.s: Un nativo las absorbió de niño; yo, con amor y tiempo.
sn.e: A native absorbed them as a child; I, with love and time.

lessons.title: Expresiones de nativo
lessons.desc: Set phrases that mark a native

sn.s: Las expresiones fijas son la firma de un nativo.
sn.e: Set expressions are a native's signature.

sn.s: 'A la postre' significa 'al final, al fin y al cabo'.
sn.e: 'A la postre' means 'in the end, after all'.

sn.s: "A la postre, todo salió bien," digo con calma.
sn.e: "In the end, everything turned out fine," I say calmly.

sn.s: 'De buenas a primeras' es 'de repente, sin aviso'.
sn.e: 'De buenas a primeras' is 'suddenly, without warning'.

sn.s: 'A ciencia cierta' es 'con total certeza'.
sn.e: 'A ciencia cierta' is 'with total certainty'.

sn.s: "No lo sé a ciencia cierta," admito con honestidad.
sn.e: "I don't know it for certain," I admit honestly.

sn.s: Hacer algo 'a regañadientes' es hacerlo de mala gana.
sn.e: Doing something 'a regañadientes' is doing it reluctantly.

sn.s: Hacer algo 'de buen grado' es hacerlo con gusto.
sn.e: Doing something 'de buen grado' is doing it willingly.

sn.s: 'A duras penas' es 'con mucha dificultad, apenas'.
sn.e: 'A duras penas' is 'barely, with great difficulty'.

sn.s: 'Por si fuera poco' añade algo más a una lista.
sn.e: 'Por si fuera poco' adds something more: 'as if that weren't enough'.

sn.s: "Llovió, y por si fuera poco, se fue la luz."
sn.e: "It rained, and as if that weren't enough, the power went out."

sn.s: 'A fin de cuentas' es 'al final, considerándolo todo'.
sn.e: 'A fin de cuentas' is 'when all's said and done'.

sn.s: Estas frases no se traducen palabra por palabra.
sn.e: These phrases aren't translated word for word.

sn.s: Se sueltan en el momento justo, como lo hace un nativo.
sn.e: They drop at just the right moment, like a native does.

sn.s: Me siento a leer el editorial del periódico.
sn.e: I sit down to read the newspaper editorial.

sn.s: Antes, este tipo de prosa me resultaba imposible.
sn.e: Before, this kind of prose was impossible for me.

sn.s: Frases largas, vocabulario denso, ideas matizadas.
sn.e: Long sentences, dense vocabulary, nuanced ideas.

sn.s: Hoy lo leo con soltura, captando cada matiz.
sn.e: Today I read it with ease, catching every nuance.

sn.s: Entiendo no solo lo que dice, sino lo que insinúa.
sn.e: I understand not just what it says, but what it implies.

sn.s: Percibo la ironía, el trasfondo, la postura del autor.
sn.e: I perceive the irony, the subtext, the author's stance.

sn.s: Reconozco los conectores cultos sin esfuerzo.
sn.e: I recognize the cultured connectors effortlessly.

sn.s: 'No obstante', 'cabe señalar', 'en última instancia'.
sn.e: 'Nonetheless', 'it's worth noting', 'ultimately'.

sn.s: Leer prensa seria es leer en el nivel más alto.
sn.e: Reading serious press is reading at the highest level.

sn.s: Interpretar un argumento complejo ya es algo natural.
sn.e: Interpreting a complex argument is now natural.

sn.s: "Comentás los editoriales mejor que yo," dice Lucía.
sn.e: "You discuss the editorials better than I do," Lucía says.

sn.s: Leer como nativo es pensar en el idioma, no traducirlo.
sn.e: Reading like a native is thinking in the language, not translating it.

sn.s: Y la prensa, antes muralla, hoy es ventana abierta.
sn.e: And the press, once a wall, is now an open window.

sn.s: El idioma escrito, en toda su hondura, ya es mío.
sn.e: The written language, in all its depth, is mine now.

sn.s: Han pasado años desde aquel primer 'buenas'.
sn.e: Years have passed since that first 'hello'.

sn.s: Aquel día llegué sin saber una sola palabra.
sn.e: That day I arrived without knowing a single word.

sn.s: Hoy pienso, sueño, amo y vivo en español.
sn.e: Today I think, dream, love, and live in Spanish.

sn.s: Lucía y yo caminamos por el mismo mercado de antes.
sn.e: Lucía and I walk through the same market as before.

sn.s: Saludo a doña Carmen, a Roberto, a los vecinos.
sn.e: I greet doña Carmen, Roberto, the neighbors.

sn.s: Cada rostro es parte de mi historia ahora.
sn.e: Each face is part of my story now.

sn.s: "¿En qué pensás?" me pregunta Lucía.
sn.e: "What are you thinking about?" Lucía asks me.

sn.s: "En el viaje. En todo lo que este idioma me dio."
sn.e: "About the journey. About all this language gave me."

sn.s: Un idioma no son solo palabras y reglas.
sn.e: A language isn't just words and rules.

sn.s: Es una puerta a un pueblo, a un amor, a un hogar.
sn.e: It's a door to a people, to a love, to a home.

sn.s: Aprender español fue aprender a pertenecer.
sn.e: Learning Spanish was learning to belong.

sn.s: Empecé buscando palabras y encontré una vida.
sn.e: I started searching for words and found a life.

sn.s: Y aunque este es el final del camino, sé una cosa.
sn.e: And though this is the end of the road, I know one thing.

sn.s: Con un idioma en el alma, uno nunca deja de empezar.
sn.e: With a language in your soul, you never stop beginning.

scenarios.title: Ordering at the fritanga
scenarios.setting: It's evening. You walk up to doña Carmen's street food stand, hungry after a long day.

steps.speaker: Doña Carmen
steps.es: ¡Hola, chele! ¿Qué te doy?
steps.en: Hi, foreigner! What can I get you?

options.feedback: Perfect — casual and friendly, using the Nica 'vos' form (tenés). She'll like that.
She'll understand you, but 'yo querer' isn't conjugated. You'd say 'quiero comida.'
That's for a taxi, not food! Watch the context.

steps.speaker: Doña Carmen
steps.es: Tengo gallo pinto, carne asada y tajadas. ¿Querés todo?
steps.en: I've got gallo pinto, grilled meat, and plantain chips. Want everything?

options.es: Dale pues, un poco de todo.
options.feedback: 'Dale pues' is the perfect Nica way to say 'okay then.' You sound local.
Polite and clear — works fine, just a little plain.
You just turned down all the food! Probably not what you wanted.

steps.speaker: Doña Carmen
steps.es: Aquí tenés. Son cuarenta córdobas.
steps.en: Here you go. That's forty córdobas.

options.feedback: Warm and respectful — calling her 'doña' is exactly right in Nicaragua.
Gets the job done, but a thank-you goes a long way here.
Forty córdobas is more than fair for a full plate — and it's a bit rude!

scenarios.title: Meeting Roberto
scenarios.desc: Introduce yourself to a new friend
scenarios.setting: You're sitting outside a pulpería when a friendly young man strikes up a conversation.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: ¡Buenas! ¿Cómo te llamás?
steps.en: Hello! What's your name?

options.en: My name is Miguel. And you?
options.feedback: Perfect — and you used 'vos,' the Nica way. Asking back keeps the conversation going.
Understandable, but a bit short. 'Me llamo Miguel' sounds warmer.
That answers 'how are you,' not 'what's your name.' Listen for the question word.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Mucho gusto, Miguel. ¿De dónde sos?
steps.en: Nice to meet you, Miguel. Where are you from?

options.feedback: Exactly right. 'Soy de' + place is how you say where you're from.
Close! But origin uses 'ser' (soy), not 'estar' (estoy). 'Soy de...'
That's your age, not where you're from. He asked '¿de dónde?'

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: ¡Qué tuani! ¿Y qué hacés aquí en Nicaragua?
steps.en: Cool! And what are you doing here in Nicaragua?

options.feedback: Clear and honest. 'Quiero' + verb is a great pattern to know.
Casual and friendly — works, though a full 'quiero aprender' is cleaner.
A missed chance to connect. Even simple Spanish keeps the conversation alive.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Pues aquí aprendés rápido. ¡Bienvenido!
steps.en: Well, you'll learn fast here. Welcome!

options.feedback: Warm and natural. Using his name makes it personal.
Polite and fine. A touch more warmth never hurts here.
A bit abrupt right after he welcomed you! A thank-you fits better.

scenarios.title: At the pharmacy
scenarios.setting: You have a headache and an upset stomach. You walk into a small farmacia.

steps.speaker: Farmacéutica
steps.es: Buenas. ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
steps.en: Hello. How can I help you?

options.feedback: Perfect. 'Me duele' + body part is exactly how you describe pain.
True and useful, but vague. Telling her what hurts gets you the right medicine faster.
This is a pharmacy, not a comedor! Tell her what's wrong.

steps.speaker: Farmacéutica
steps.es: ¿Y también le duele el estómago?
steps.en: And does your stomach hurt too?

options.feedback: Simple and clear. 'Un poco' is a handy way to soften an answer.
Fine — though a word or two more helps her help you.
Honest, and a perfectly good thing to say when stuck! She'll rephrase.

steps.speaker: Farmacéutica
steps.es: Le doy estas pastillas. Una cada ocho horas.
steps.en: I'll give you these pills. One every eight hours.

options.feedback: Always good to ask the price. Clear and practical.
A fine clarifying question if you missed it — never be afraid to ask.
You came in sick — turning down the medicine leaves you no better off!

steps.speaker: Farmacéutica
steps.es: Cuarenta córdobas. Que se mejore.
steps.en: Forty córdobas. Get well soon.

options.feedback: Lovely. 'Muy amable' is a warm, very Nica way to thank someone.
Perfectly fine and polite.
Forty córdobas for medicine is fair — and you don't haggle at a pharmacy!

scenarios.title: Taking a taxi
scenarios.desc: Get across town and agree on a price
scenarios.setting: You flag down a taxi on a busy Managua street. You need to get to the UCA university.

steps.speaker: Chofer
steps.es: ¿Para dónde vas?
steps.en: Where are you headed?

options.feedback: Clear destination, polite. Exactly what he needs to hear.
Also great — 'voy a' + place is a solid, natural pattern.
He can't drive you nowhere! You need to name a destination.

steps.speaker: Chofer
steps.es: Te llevo por cien córdobas.
steps.en: I'll take you for a hundred córdobas.

options.feedback: Taxis in Managua aren't metered — negotiating is normal and expected.
You can accept, but the first price is usually negotiable. No harm trying.
Dollars, not córdobas?! That's a huge overpay. He said córdobas.

steps.speaker: Chofer
steps.es: Bueno, ochenta. Pero subí rápido.
steps.en: Fine, eighty. But get in quick.

options.feedback: 'Dale pues' seals a deal perfectly — you sound like a local.
Clear agreement. Confirming the number avoids confusion later.
If you truly didn't catch it, fine to ask — but he means córdobas.

steps.speaker: Chofer
steps.es: Listo. Llegamos. Son ochenta.
steps.en: Done. We're here. That's eighty.

options.es: Aquí tiene. Que le vaya bien.
options.feedback: Smooth and warm. 'Que le vaya bien' is the perfect parting line.
Clear and polite — hands over the fare with thanks.
After agreeing to the fare? That's a problem you don't want to create!

scenarios.title: At the market
scenarios.setting: You're at the bustling Mercado Oriental. A vendor calls out as you pass her fruit stand.

steps.speaker: Vendedora
steps.es: ¡Buenas! Pase, pase. ¿Qué va a llevar?
steps.en: Hello! Come, come. What will you take?

options.feedback: Great opener. Asking the price first is exactly how you start.
Clear enough, though naming what you want gets you served faster.
A totally valid thing to say! Perfectly polite to browse.

steps.speaker: Vendedora
steps.es: Las naranjas están a cinco por veinte córdobas.
steps.en: The oranges are five for twenty córdobas.

options.feedback: 'Deme' (give me) is the natural way to order at a stand. Clean.
Also perfect — clear quantity and item.
Yes to what? She needs to know how many you want.

steps.speaker: Vendedora
steps.es: ¿Algo más, mi amor? Tengo mangos bien dulces.
steps.en: Anything else, dear? I have really sweet mangos.

options.feedback: 'Así está bien' is a smooth way to say 'that's enough.' Very natural.
Gets the point across, but feels a little blunt. A 'gracias' softens it.
Why not! Clear and confident. The mangos really are good there.

steps.speaker: Vendedora
steps.es: Son veinte córdobas. Gracias, mi amor.
steps.en: That's twenty córdobas. Thank you, dear.

options.es: Aquí tiene. Que tenga buen día.
options.en: Here you go. Have a good day.
options.feedback: Warm and complete. A good-day wish lands well in the market.
Lovely touch — 'gracias a usted' returns the warmth politely.
Twenty córdobas for fruit is fair — and grumbling sours a friendly exchange.

scenarios.title: Haggling for a shirt
scenarios.desc: Negotiate a price at the market
scenarios.setting: At the market you spot a shirt you like. The vendor notices your interest.

steps.speaker: Vendedor
steps.es: Esa camisa le queda bien. Doscientos córdobas.
steps.en: That shirt suits you. Two hundred córdobas.

options.es: Está un poco caro. ¿No hay rebaja?
options.en: It's a bit pricey. Any discount?
options.feedback: Textbook haggling — polite, but you opened the negotiation. Expected here.
You can accept, but the first price almost always has room. Try a counter.
If you don't want it, fine — but you said you liked it. Mixed signals.

steps.speaker: Vendedor
steps.es: Para vos, ciento setenta. Es buen precio.
steps.en: For you, one seventy. It's a good price.

options.feedback: A confident counter-offer. Meeting in the middle is the whole game.
Fair enough — you can settle here. But one more nudge often works.
Walking away is a valid tactic — sometimes they call you back with a better price!

steps.speaker: Vendedor
steps.es: Uy, me estás matando. Ciento cincuenta y es tuya.
steps.en: Oof, you're killing me. One fifty and it's yours.

options.feedback: Deal sealed with a perfect 'dale pues.' You haggled like a local.
Clear acceptance — 'la llevo' (I'll take it) is exactly right.
Pushing too hard after a fair drop can kill the deal. Know when to close.

steps.speaker: Vendedor
steps.es: Buena compra. Te la pongo en una bolsa.
steps.en: Good buy. I'll put it in a bag for you.

options.feedback: Friendly close. A good haggle ends with everyone smiling.
Perfectly fine.

options.en: I hope it doesn't fall apart.
options.feedback: A little insulting after he gave you a deal! Better to keep it warm.

scenarios.title: Asking for directions
scenarios.setting: You're lost looking for a friend's house. You stop a friendly woman on the sidewalk.

steps.speaker: Señora
steps.es: ¿Andás perdido, muchacho?
steps.en: Are you lost, young man?

options.es: Sí, busco la casa azul cerca del parque.
options.en: Yes, I'm looking for the blue house near the park.
options.feedback: Perfect — you gave a landmark, which is exactly how directions work here.
Honest! But tell her where you're trying to go so she can help.
But you ARE lost — let her help! Pride won't get you there.

steps.speaker: Señora
steps.es: Ah, sí. De aquí, dos cuadras arriba.
steps.en: Ah, yes. From here, two blocks east.

options.feedback: Smart question! 'Arriba' = east (where the sun rises) confuses every newcomer.
Okay — but make sure you know which way 'arriba' is, or you'll go wrong.
Not 'up'! In Nica directions 'arriba' means east, not upward.

steps.speaker: Señora
steps.es: Exacto. Después una cuadra al sur, en la esquina.
steps.en: Exactly. Then one block south, on the corner.

options.es: Dos arriba y una al sur. ¿Verdad?
options.en: Two east and one south. Right?
options.feedback: Repeating directions back is the best way to lock them in. Smart move.
Hope you've got it! Confirming would've been safer.
No shame in that — though most folks here just point and tell.

steps.speaker: Señora
steps.es: Así es. Que Dios te acompañe, muchacho.
steps.en: That's it. May God go with you, young man.

options.feedback: Warm and respectful. 'Señora' shows the right courtesy.
Nice — returning her blessing is a lovely touch.
A bit flat after such a kind send-off, but it works.

scenarios.title: Catching the bus
scenarios.desc: Ride the urban bus and pay the fare
scenarios.setting: A crowded bus pulls up. You squeeze on and the cobrador (fare collector) works his way toward you.

steps.speaker: Cobrador
steps.es: ¡Pasaje, pasaje! ¿Para dónde, joven?
steps.en: Fare, fare! Where to, young man?

options.feedback: Destination plus the fare question — efficient, exactly right for a packed bus.
Good — he'll tell you the fare. Asking the price yourself is even smoother.
On a moving bus he needs a quick answer. Have your stop ready.

steps.speaker: Cobrador
steps.es: Cinco córdobas.
steps.en: Five córdobas.

options.feedback: Quick and clear — hand over the coins and you're set.

options.en: Do you have change for a hundred?
options.feedback: Fair to ask, but small bills are gold on buses. Try to have coins ready.
Five córdobas is the fixed fare — there's no haggling on the bus!

steps.speaker: Señora a la par
steps.es: Agárrese bien, que este chofer maneja recio.
steps.en: Hold on tight, this driver drives hard.

options.feedback: Friendly — strangers look out for each other on the bus. Accept the kindness.
Nice, natural reply — shares the moment with a little humor.
Yikes — she's being kind! That would be rude here, where buses are social.

steps.speaker: Cobrador
steps.es: ¡Centro! El que se baja, que se baje ya.
steps.en: Downtown! Whoever's getting off, get off now.

options.feedback: 'Permiso' to squeeze past the crowd is essential bus etiquette. Perfect.
Clear and loud enough to be heard — just what's needed.
The bus won't wait! You have to move quickly at your stop.

scenarios.title: Ordering lunch
scenarios.desc: Order a full meal at a comedor
scenarios.setting: It's lunchtime. You sit down at a small comedor and the cook comes over.

steps.speaker: Cocinera
steps.es: Buenas. Hoy hay carne asada o pollo. ¿Qué le sirvo?
steps.en: Hello. Today there's grilled beef or chicken. What can I serve you?

options.feedback: Clear choice, polite. Exactly what she's waiting to hear.
Great question — shows you're curious about the meal. Comes with gallo pinto and more.
She'll pick for you, but stating a choice is friendlier and gets you what you want.

steps.speaker: Cocinera
steps.es: Viene con gallo pinto, maduro y ensalada. ¿Y de tomar?
steps.en: It comes with gallo pinto, fried plantain, and salad. And to drink?

options.es: Un fresco de cacao, por favor.
options.feedback: Perfect — ordering a típico fresco like a local. Cacao is a classic.

options.en: What fresh drinks do you have?
options.feedback: Always good to ask — Nica frescos are a highlight worth exploring.
Fine, though a cold fresco with lunch is half the joy here!

steps.speaker: Cocinera
steps.es: Aquí tiene. Buen provecho.
steps.en: Here you go. Enjoy your meal.

options.feedback: Warm and appreciative — cooks love to hear the food looks good.
Polite and perfectly fine.
It's a generous plate! That would come off as ungrateful.

steps.speaker: Cocinera
steps.es: ¿Le gustó? ¿Le traigo algo más?
steps.en: Did you like it? Can I bring you anything else?

options.es: Me encantó, gracias. La cuenta, por favor.
options.en: I loved it, thanks. The check, please.
options.feedback: Full and natural — compliment plus asking for the bill. Smooth finish.

options.en: It was really good. Nothing else.
options.feedback: Lovely — 'estaba rico' is exactly how you praise a meal.
Yes to which part? A fuller answer helps her.

scenarios.title: Making plans
scenarios.setting: Roberto calls you. He wants to make plans for the weekend.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: ¿Qué hacés el sábado? Vamos a la playa.
steps.en: What are you doing Saturday? Let's go to the beach.

options.feedback: Enthusiastic and natural. 'Dale' is the perfect way to say yes here.
Practical — getting the details before committing is totally normal.
True, but it's a flat reply to a fun invite. Show some interest!

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Salimos temprano, como a las seis de la mañana.
steps.en: We leave early, around six in the morning.

options.feedback: Natural reaction plus agreement — sounds like a real friend chatting.
Clear confirmation of the time. No confusion later.

options.es: Las seis de la tarde, bien.
options.feedback: He said morning (de la mañana)! You'd miss the whole trip.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Nos vemos en mi casa. No llegués tarde.
steps.en: Meet at my house. Don't be late.

options.feedback: Reassuring and easy — 'tranquilo' is a very Nica way to say no worries.
Short, confident, reliable. Good.
Not the thing to say after he asked you not to be late!

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Tuani. Entonces nos vemos el sábado, pues.
steps.en: Cool. So we'll see each other Saturday, then.

options.feedback: Warm sign-off between friends. Exactly the right register.
Casual and friendly — 'ahí nos vemos' is perfect for closing plans.
'Señor'?! Way too formal for a friend. Keep it casual with Roberto.

scenarios.title: Talking about yourself
scenarios.desc: Share your life with a new friend
scenarios.setting: At a gathering, someone you just met is curious about you and starts asking questions.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: Y vos, ¿de qué trabajás?
steps.en: And you, what do you do for work?

options.en: I'm a programmer. I work with computers.
options.feedback: Clear and complete. 'Soy' + profession is exactly right.
That dodges the question! She wants to know what you do.
Understandable, just a little terse. A full sentence feels warmer.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¡Qué interesante! ¿Y tenés familia aquí?
steps.en: How interesting! And do you have family here?

options.es: No, mi familia vive en Estados Unidos.
options.en: No, my family lives in the US.
options.feedback: Natural and honest. 'Vive en' tells her where they are.

options.es: Tengo dos hermanos, pero viven lejos.
options.en: I have two siblings, but they live far away.
options.feedback: Lovely detail — sharing a little extra invites connection.
A 'yes' with no detail closes the door. Give her something to follow up on.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¿Y te hallás aquí en Nicaragua?
steps.en: And do you feel at home here in Nicaragua?

options.es: Me encanta. La gente es muy cálida.
options.en: I love it. The people are very warm.
options.feedback: A warm answer that compliments her people — that lands beautifully.
Honest, but a bit flat. If you do like it, let it show!

options.es: Sí me hallo, gracias a la gente.
options.en: Yes I feel at home, thanks to the people.
options.feedback: Great — you even reused her word 'hallar.' Sounds very natural.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: Pues ya sos uno más de nosotros.
steps.en: Well, you're one of us now.

options.es: Eso me hace muy feliz. Gracias.
options.en: That makes me very happy. Thanks.
options.feedback: Heartfelt and natural. A perfect response to being welcomed in.
'Igualmente' doesn't quite fit here — there's nothing to return. A simple thanks is better.
Pleasant, but a warmer reply would honor the kind thing she said.

scenarios.title: How was your weekend?
scenarios.setting: It's Monday morning. Your coworker wants to hear about your weekend.

steps.speaker: Compañero
steps.es: ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana?
steps.en: What did you do over the weekend?

options.es: Fui a la playa con unos amigos.
options.en: I went to the beach with some friends.
options.feedback: Past tense nailed — 'fui' (I went) is the one to know. Great.
That's present tense — sounds like a plan, not what happened. He asked about the past.
He'll get the gist, but a full sentence shows off your past tense.

steps.speaker: Compañero
steps.es: ¡Qué rico! ¿Y qué tal estuvo?
steps.en: Nice! And how was it?

options.en: It was a lot of fun. I swam a lot.
options.feedback: 'Estuvo' and 'nadé' — two past forms in one breath. You're getting it.
Present tense again — try 'estuvo' (it was) for something that's done.

options.en: Lots of fun, I ate fish.
options.feedback: Nice — 'comí' (I ate) is perfect. Casual and clear.

steps.speaker: Compañero
steps.es: ¿Y el domingo qué tal?
steps.en: And how about Sunday?

options.es: Descansé en casa y vi una película.
options.en: I rested at home and watched a movie.
options.feedback: Two more clean past verbs. You're telling a real story now.
Short but correct — 'descansé' is spot on. Totally natural.
That's a habit (present). He asked about THIS Sunday — try 'descansé.'

steps.speaker: Compañero
steps.es: Suena a un buen fin de semana.
steps.en: Sounds like a good weekend.

options.es: Sí, la verdad estuvo bien. ¿Y el tuyo?
options.en: Yeah, honestly it was good. And yours?
options.feedback: Perfect close — you answered AND turned it back to him. Real conversation.
Fine — though asking about his weekend would keep it flowing.
A bit of a conversation-ender. Toss the question back to him!

scenarios.title: Dinner at a friend's house
scenarios.setting: You've been invited to Roberto's home for dinner. His mother greets you at the door.

steps.speaker: Doña Rosa
steps.es: ¡Pase, pase! Qué bueno que vino.
steps.en: Come in, come in! So glad you came.

options.en: Thank you for inviting me, ma'am.
options.feedback: Gracious and respectful — 'doña' is just the right touch of warmth.
Too casual for a host welcoming you in. A thank-you sets the right tone.
Ha! Playful and charming — Nica hosts love a guest ready to eat.

steps.speaker: Doña Rosa
steps.es: Siéntese. Hice gallo pinto y carne. Coma, coma.
steps.en: Sit down. I made gallo pinto and meat. Eat, eat.

options.en: It looks delicious. Thank you, ma'am.
options.feedback: Complimenting the food before eating delights any cook. Perfect.
Ouch — she cooked for you! That would hurt her feelings here.
Polite, though she'll likely insist on serving you a generous plate herself.

steps.speaker: Doña Rosa
steps.es: ¿Le gustó? ¿Quiere más?
steps.en: Did you like it? Want more?

options.es: Estaba delicioso. Un poquito más, gracias.
options.en: It was delicious. A little more, thanks.
options.feedback: Accepting seconds is a compliment in itself. 'Estaba delicioso' is perfect past tense.

options.es: Sí, todo muy rico. Ya quedé lleno.
options.en: Yes, all delicious. I'm full now.
options.feedback: Gracious either way — praising the food while gently declining more is smooth.
'Just okay' about a home-cooked meal? That stings. Always praise the cook.

steps.speaker: Doña Rosa
steps.es: Aquí siempre tiene su plato, mijo.
steps.en: Here you always have your plate, dear.

options.es: Eso significa mucho para mí. Gracias.
options.en: That means a lot to me. Thank you.
options.feedback: Heartfelt — she just treated you like family, and you honored it.
Warm and respectful. A lovely way to receive her generosity.
Way too abrupt after such a tender thing to say! Meet warmth with warmth.

scenarios.title: What do you like?
scenarios.setting: At a relaxed hangout, the conversation turns to music, hobbies, and what everyone's into.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¿Qué te gusta hacer en tu tiempo libre?
steps.en: What do you like to do in your free time?

options.es: Me gusta leer y salir a caminar.
options.en: I like to read and go for walks.
options.feedback: 'Me gusta' + verb, two activities — exactly how to talk about hobbies.
Like what? The sentence needs what you like — 'me gusta leer,' for example.

options.en: Reading, walking, that kind of thing.
options.feedback: Casual and clear enough — a full 'me gusta' would be a touch smoother.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¿Y te gusta la música? ¿Qué escuchás?
steps.en: And do you like music? What do you listen to?

options.es: Me encanta la música. Escucho de todo.
options.en: I love music. I listen to everything.
options.feedback: 'Me encanta' is stronger than 'me gusta' — great for things you really love.
Totally valid if true! Just unusual — be ready for a surprised look.
She wants to know WHICH music. Name a kind to keep it going.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¿Sabés bailar? Aquí todos bailan.
steps.en: Do you know how to dance? Everyone dances here.

options.es: Un poco, pero no muy bien.
options.en: A little, but not very well.
options.feedback: Honest and humble — and it invites them to teach you, which they'll love.

options.en: No, but I want to learn.
options.feedback: Even better — showing you want to learn opens the door to connection.
Bold! Be ready to back that up — they'll absolutely call your bluff.

steps.speaker: Karla
steps.es: ¡Entonces te enseñamos! Vení.
steps.en: Then we'll teach you! Come on.

options.en: Okay! But be patient with me.
options.feedback: Playful and willing — 'dale' plus humor is the perfect yes.

options.en: Alright, let's give it a try.
options.feedback: Game and easygoing. 'Vamos a intentarlo' fits the moment well.
Turning down the invite shuts down a warm moment. Jump in — that's where friendship grows!

scenarios.title: A heart-to-heart
scenarios.desc: Open up about a hard day
scenarios.setting: You've had a rough day. Roberto can tell something's off and asks about it.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Te veo medio raro. ¿Qué te pasa?
steps.en: You seem a bit off. What's wrong?

options.es: Tuve un mal día, la verdad.
options.en: I had a bad day, honestly.
options.feedback: Open and natural — 'la verdad' (honestly) makes it feel real and trusting.
We all say it, but he can tell. It's okay to let a friend in.

options.es: Estoy cansado y un poco triste.
options.en: I'm tired and a little sad.
options.feedback: Naming feelings directly — exactly the Phase 2 leap. Honest and clear.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Contame, pues. ¿Qué pasó?
steps.en: Tell me, then. What happened?

options.es: Perdí mi teléfono y llegué tarde al trabajo.
options.en: I lost my phone and got to work late.
options.feedback: Two past-tense verbs telling a real story — 'perdí' and 'llegué.' Strong.

options.en: A lot of things went wrong today.
options.feedback: Nice — 'salieron mal' (went wrong) is a useful, natural phrase.
Valid to feel that way — though he's offering an ear, and that's worth something.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Uy, qué mala onda. ¿Y cómo te sentís ahora?
steps.en: Oof, that's rough. And how do you feel now?

options.feedback: Honest about the feeling AND grateful for the talk. Beautifully balanced.

options.es: Un poco mejor, gracias por escuchar.
options.en: A little better, thanks for listening.
options.feedback: Warm and real — acknowledging his support is exactly right.
Honest — and that's okay. A good friend won't rush you to feel better.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Tranquilo, hermano. Mañana es otro día.
steps.en: Easy, brother. Tomorrow's another day.

options.feedback: Returning 'hermano' seals the bond — that's deep friendship in Nica terms.
Touching and sincere. This is what Phase 2 is all about — real connection.
He's being a true friend — a warmer reply honors that better.

scenarios.title: Making a complaint
scenarios.setting: The fan you bought last week stopped working. You return to the store with your receipt.

steps.speaker: Empleada
steps.es: Buenas. ¿En qué le ayudo?
steps.en: Hello. How can I help you?

options.es: Compré este ventilador y ya no funciona.
options.en: I bought this fan and it no longer works.
options.feedback: Clear and factual — states the problem without aggression. Exactly right.
Starting hostile puts her on the defensive. Calm and factual gets better results.

options.en: I have a problem with this.
options.feedback: Okay, but vague. Saying what's actually wrong moves things faster.

steps.speaker: Empleada
steps.es: ¿Tiene el recibo y cuánto hace que lo compró?
steps.en: Do you have the receipt, and how long ago did you buy it?

options.es: Sí, aquí está. Lo compré hace una semana.
options.en: Yes, here it is. I bought it a week ago.
options.feedback: Receipt plus a clear timeframe — you're making her job easy. Perfect.
Harder without it, but worth trying. Bring the receipt when you can.

options.en: A long time ago, I don't remember.
options.feedback: Vague timing weakens your case — and warranties have limits. Be specific.

steps.speaker: Empleada
steps.es: Déjeme revisar. ¿Qué solución busca usted?
steps.en: Let me check. What solution are you looking for?

options.es: Quiero un cambio o que me devuelvan el dinero.
options.en: I want an exchange or my money back.
options.feedback: Stating your desired outcome clearly is exactly how to resolve a complaint.
Polite, but naming what you want protects your interest. Don't be shy here.

options.en: I don't know, you tell me.
options.feedback: Hands her all the power. Knowing your ask gives you footing.

steps.speaker: Empleada
steps.es: Tiene razón, está en garantía. Le doy uno nuevo.
steps.en: You're right, it's under warranty. I'll give you a new one.

options.es: Se lo agradezco mucho. Muy amable.
options.en: I appreciate it very much. Very kind.
options.feedback: Gracious in victory — leaving on good terms is smart and warm.

options.es: Por fin. Debió ser más rápido.
options.feedback: She just helped you! Souring it at the end burns goodwill you may need again.
Clean and polite. A satisfying close to a complaint handled well.

scenarios.title: At the bank
scenarios.setting: You've waited in line at the bank. It's your turn at the teller's window.

steps.speaker: Cajero
steps.es: Buenos días. ¿En qué le puedo servir?
steps.en: Good morning. How can I help you?

options.es: Quisiera abrir una cuenta, por favor.
options.en: I'd like to open an account, please.
options.feedback: 'Quisiera' (I'd like) is the polished, formal way to ask. Perfect for a bank.
Way too blunt for a formal setting — and 'dame' is too casual here.
Understandable, just abrupt. A full polite sentence fits the bank better.

steps.speaker: Cajero
steps.es: Con gusto. ¿Trae algún documento de identidad?
steps.en: Gladly. Do you have an ID document?

options.feedback: Direct and prepared. Exactly what he needs to proceed.
A smart question if unsure — better to ask than to be turned away.
You can't open an account with no ID. Always bring documents to the bank.

steps.speaker: Cajero
steps.es: Perfecto. Llene este formulario y firme abajo.
steps.en: Perfect. Fill out this form and sign below.

options.feedback: Asking to be sure before signing anything official is exactly the right instinct.
Fine if you're sure — but on official forms, confirming where never hurts.

options.en: I don't like filling out forms.
options.feedback: Relatable! But it's required — best to just work through it politely.

steps.speaker: Cajero
steps.es: Todo en orden. Su cuenta estará activa mañana.
steps.en: Everything's in order. Your account will be active tomorrow.

options.en: Thank you very much for your help.
options.feedback: Polite and warm — the right note to end a formal interaction on.
Next-day activation is normal. Complaining about it just sours things.
Smooth and courteous. A good-day wish is always welcome.

scenarios.title: Clearing the air
scenarios.desc: Resolve a misunderstanding with a friend
scenarios.setting: Roberto has been short with you all day. You sense something's wrong and decide to address it.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Dijiste que venías ayer y nunca llegaste.
steps.en: You said you were coming yesterday and never showed up.

options.es: Creo que hubo un malentendido. Yo entendí hoy.
options.en: I think there was a misunderstanding. I understood today.
options.feedback: Naming it as a misunderstanding (not blaming) opens the door to fixing it calmly.
Flat denial escalates things. Even if you're sure, lead with curiosity, not defense.
Honest if true — but if it was really a mix-up, say so rather than take false blame.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: ¿En serio? Yo te dije bien claro que era ayer.
steps.en: Really? I told you clearly it was yesterday.

options.es: Puede que no te entendí bien. Disculpá.
options.en: Maybe I didn't understand you well. Sorry.
options.feedback: Taking partial responsibility cools things without grovelling. Very mature.
Turning it into blame reignites the conflict. The goal is to repair, not win.
Brushing it off can feel dismissive when he's clearly bothered. Acknowledge his feeling.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Bueno, tal vez los dos nos confundimos.
steps.en: Well, maybe we both got confused.

options.en: Surely. The important thing is to clear it up.
options.feedback: Refocusing on resolution over fault — exactly how to close a misunderstanding.

options.es: Sí, no quiero que quedemos mal por esto.
options.en: Yes, I don't want us to be on bad terms over this.
options.feedback: Naming that you value the friendship is warm and disarming. Beautiful.
Dismissive — he just offered an olive branch. Meet it, don't swat it away.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Tenés razón. Todo bien, hermano.
steps.en: You're right. All good, brother.

options.en: All good. Thanks for talking it out.
options.feedback: Appreciating the conversation itself strengthens the bond. Perfect close.

options.en: Done. Next time I'll confirm clearly.
options.feedback: Owning a small fix going forward shows real maturity. Nicely done.
A jab at the end undoes the repair. End warm when someone offers peace.

scenarios.title: Asking a big favor
scenarios.setting: Your laptop broke right before a deadline. You call Roberto to ask for serious help.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: ¿Aló? ¿Qué pasó, todo bien?
steps.en: Hello? What's up, everything okay?

options.es: Roberto, ¿te puedo pedir un favor grande?
options.en: Roberto, can I ask you a big favor?
options.feedback: Signaling upfront that it's a big ask is courteous — it lets him prepare.
Demanding, not asking. A big favor needs a softer, more respectful opener.
Polite, though a touch over-apologetic. Friends don't need so much hedging.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Claro, decime. ¿Qué necesitás?
steps.en: Of course, tell me. What do you need?

options.es: ¿Me podrías prestar tu laptop unos días?
options.en: Could you lend me your laptop for a few days?
options.feedback: 'Podrías' (could you) is the soft, polite conditional — ideal for a real favor.
Direct command — fine between close friends, but 'podrías' lands softer for a big ask.
'Give me' sounds like you're keeping it! And it's too demanding. Ask to borrow, gently.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Uy, la uso para el trabajo... ¿para cuándo la necesitás?
steps.en: Oof, I use it for work... when do you need it?

options.es: Solo hasta el viernes. Te la cuido bien.
options.en: Just until Friday. I'll take good care of it.
options.feedback: Specific timeframe plus reassurance — you're addressing his exact worry. Excellent.
Vague timing on someone's work computer? That'll make him hesitate. Be precise.

options.es: Entiendo si no podés, no hay problema.
options.en: I understand if you can't, no problem.
options.feedback: Gracious — giving him an out is kind, though you can still make your case first.

steps.speaker: Roberto
steps.es: Está bien, confío en vos. Pasá por ella.
steps.en: Alright, I trust you. Come get it.

options.es: De verdad te lo agradezco un montón.
options.en: I really appreciate it a ton.
options.feedback: Heartfelt thanks for a real favor — and it honors the trust he just showed.

options.en: Thanks, brother. I owe you one.
options.feedback: 'Te debo una' (I owe you one) is perfect — warm and acknowledges the favor.
A bit flat for someone lending you their work laptop. A real thanks fits better.

scenarios.title: The job interview
